title: Introduction
content:
Hubzero® is an open source software platform for building powerful websites that host analytical tools, publish data, share resources, collaborate and build communities in a single web-based ecosystem. Initially created by researchers in the NSF-sponsored Network for Computational Nanotechnology to support nanoHUB.org. The Hubzero Platform now supports science gateways from a variety of disciplines with a collective of over 2 million visitors a year.

Hubzero includes a powerful content management system built to support scientific activities. Members on a hub can write blog entries, participate in discussion groups, work together in projects, publish datasets and computational tools with digital object identifiers (DOIs), and make these publications available for others to use—not as dusty downloads, but as live, interactive digital resources. Simulation/modeling tools published on a hub can be accessed with the click of a button, running on cloud computing resources, campus clusters, and other national high-performance computing (HPC) facilities and serve up compelling visualizations.

Hubzero partners to help researchers:

  • Create datasets and interactive simulation tools using RStudio, Jupyter Notebooks, and other Web Applications
  • Publish research products including, datasets, tools, and white papers, through a step-by-step guided system
  • Provide spaces for your research teams and collaborators to discuss data concepts, track progress, and share files.

 

We are no longer able to support the Hubzero Platform as a complete open source product. Please see https://hubzero.org for hosting options or email info@hubzero.org. 

We are in the process of releasing a self service, self-hosted Hubzero CMS product here to explore before trying one of our hosting or development services. This will not include many integrations including tools. This is a work in progress.

title: Invoke scripts for Jupyter notebooks
content:
Invoke scripts for Jupyter notebooks

The hub tool invoke script is located in the tool's middleware/ subdirectory. When you first create a tool, the basic invoke script provided must be edited to work with Jupyter notebook tools.

This writeup shows you how to create Jupyter tools with three different appearances: notebook, App, and Tool mode.

invoke_app and start_jupyter

To deploy a Jupyter notebook as a tool on your hub, you call the invoke_app executable, which in turn calls start_jupyter. Each have their own arguments:

arguments for start_jupyter

  -h, --help  show this help message and exit.
  -d          Show debug (verbose) output.
  -t          Run as a Tool with no notebook controls.
  -c          Copy instead of link notebook files.
  -A          Run in AppMode.
  -T dir      Search for notebook starting in dir.
  --themes    Enable notebook themes

arguments for invoke_app

  -t Tool name
  -C command to execute
  -r Rappture version to use (normally specify none for notebook tools)
  -w headless
  -u environment package (repeat as necessary)

invoke_app: starting point

The basic invoke script for Jupyter notebooks looks like this:

/usr/bin/invoke_app "$@" -t TOOLNAME \
	                 -C "start_jupyter -T @tool APP.ipynb" \
	                 -r none \
                         -w headless \
	                 -u anaconda-X

Invoking a Jupyter tool this way gives a notebook with all its code cells displayed to the user.

Where:

  • TOOLNAME is the short name of the tool
  • APP is the name of the main notebook that runs the tool
  • anaconda-X is the current anaconda installation

start_jupyter arguments

Control the way the notebook appears when run as a tool, using the arguments passed to the start_jupyter executable.

You can run a Jupyter tool in three ways:

  • notebook mode, in which all code cells are displayed to the user (shown above)
  • app mode, in which code cells are initially hidden but can be displayed
  • tool mode, in which code cells are hidden and cannot be displayed
for App Mode

For a notebook tool that hides its code cells and shows only the UI and markdown elements on initial run, add the -A argument in the start_jupyter call:

/usr/bin/invoke_app "$@" -t TOOLNAME \
	                 -C "start_jupyter -A -T @tool APP.ipynb" \
	                 -u anaconda-X \
                         -w headless \
	                 -r none

The tool user can toggle the tool's "Edit App" button to show the underlying code cells, making this a great teaching/demo option.


NOTE that this differs from the invoke_app -A argument.

for Tool Mode
 

To permanently hide code cells from the user in App Mode, specify the -A and -t arguments in the start_jupyter call:

/usr/bin/invoke_app "$@" -t TOOLNAME \
	                 -C "start_jupyter -A -t -T @tool APP.ipynb" \
	                 -u anaconda-X \
                         -w headless \
	                 -r none

The Edit App button will not be displayed to the tool user.     
    
NOTE that this differs from the invoke_app -t argument.

errors

specify no rappture
/usr/bin/invoke_app "$@" -t TOOLNAME \
	                 -C "start_jupyter -T @tool APP.ipynb" \
	                 -u anaconda-X \
                         -w headless \
	                 -r none
Error:

Running the tool's invoke script from a workspace, returns:

"could not find a rappture installation: RAPPTURE_PATH=,"
Fix:

Be sure to supply the "-r none" argument in the invoke_app call, as above. No quotation marks are needed.

title: Environment Variables
content:
Environment variables

A number of environment variables are available in a hub tool session. A few are discussed here. A full list can be viewed by running the env command from a terminal in the Workspace tool, the noVNC Desktop, or the Terminal.

Remember: tools are invoked by the current user's account and all permissions are set accordingly. Therefore, a tool can save files to a user's home directory, because the tool runs as that user.

SESSION

This variable stores the session ID or session number of the currently running tool.  It's the ID of the session you are currently using. You can assume it's unique.

Notice that your current SESSION number is visible in your browser URL when you are running a tool. Here's an example:

https://proxy.yourhub.org/weber/20064/...

USER

The USER variable stores the username of the user running the current tool.

SESSIONDIR

The SESSIONDIR variable stores the current session directory of the current tool run.  A separate directory is created for each new tool session. Since it is created in the current user's home directory, the tool can write to this directory.

This is the recommended location for writing temporary files generated by your tool. Be mindful of the user's quota limits when writing temporary results. It's wise to delete these once the run is complete.

Session directories take the form:

/home/HUBNAME/USER/data/sessions/SESSION
RESULTSDIR

The RESULTSDIR variable stores the results directory for the current tool run. It is located in the user's home directory. This is a good place to place simulation results and output for the user to access later.

Be mindful of the user's quota limits when writing results.

Results directories take the form:

/home/HUBNAME/USER/data/results/SESSION
PWD

This variable stores the present working directory.

HOME

This variable stores the full path to the user's home directory.  This can be useful if a tool provides an option to save the user's current work. Tool developers should create a directory for the tool to save files relative to HOME, to prevent cluttering the user's home directory. For example, "$HOME/data/toolname".

Note that unlike the RESULTSDIR and SESSIONDIR described above, "$HOME/data/toolname" will not be created for each tool run.

Home directories take the form:

/home/HUBNAME/USER

Accessing environment variables on a hub

For a full list of environment variables, type this in a Workspace terminal:

printenv

To view the value of an environment variable from the Workspace terminal (sh or bash shell, e.g.):

echo $SESSION

From Jupyter's Python kernel, for example, use the shell escape:

!echo $SESSION

title: Testing Jupyter-based tools
content:
Testing Jupyter-based tools

The proxied Jupyter tool is a useful place to develop code and analyses in a notebook style. Hub users can easily share their notebooks with other users by publishing notebooks as tools. 

These instructions take you through testing the deployment of a Jupyter notebook based tool. Here, we'll assume that the short name for your tool is toolname. To test the notebook tool, it's handy to use the hub's Workspace tool, since this allows you to fully test the deployment in the context of the hub.

1. Create the tool

Once you have your notebook working to your satisfaction on the hub, you next create the tool to house it, and edit the invoke script. Once this is done, it is time to test.

NOTE that any new development, and any updates to existing tools, should make use of Debian10 containers. Develop these using the appropriate Jupyter tool and Workspace10.

2. Test invoke the tool

From the Workspace10 tool, or the Jupyter terminal tool, navigate to the directory where your tool's repo is located. For a tool you've called toolname and stored in the apps subdirectory of your home, this will be something like:

~/apps/toolname

Now, navigate to your tool's middleware directory, and call the invoke script for your tool, by typing:

cd middleware
./invoke

Check the command line output to determine the success of your tool invoke call. Errors will display here if a problem is encountered. Use these to aid in your troubleshooting. If you see errors, you will need to revisit the tool sources, retesting to see if your fixes have worked, before going on with this procedure. Note that you may also see warnings displayed, as well as informational output. Neither warnings nor information indicate issues that need to be fixed.

A successful invoke script call will output in part:

The Jupyter notebook is running

...followed by a lengthy URL that reads, in part:

https://proxy.yourhub.org/weber/

Congratulations, your notebook-based tool is now running!

3. Check the running notebook

In the Workspace10 tool's command line output, note the informational output, denoted by lines starting in "I", and warning output, denoted by lines starting in "W", that is also displayed. These messages can be ignored safely; refer to the figure below.

Within the Workspace10 tool, you can now start a browser and paste into it the URL of the running Jupyter kernel. This test is not possible from outside your development environment, in order to protect your unreleased tool.

Copy the running kernel's URL

First, locate and highlight the kernel URL provided in the output from the invoke script.

Start the Workspace10 browser

Start the Firefox browser from the Workspace tool's menu. To do so, click the black button at the bottom left of the Workspace10 and access the Firefox menu item.

Navigate to the running kernel

A browser window will display, running inside your Workspace tool session on your hub. Finally, click (mouse wheel or both mouse buttons) to paste the running Jupyter kernel's URL into the browser navigation bar, as shown in this graphic

Now, the Workspace browser will display the running tool. This is the notebook running as a tool, and should be a good indication of how the tool will run once it is deployed.

One important error type you should watch for is the URL timeout. If there are URLs that your notebook needs access to in order to run, they will likely time out during this test. Collect any such URLs and include them in a support ticket on your hub to your hub administrators. The administrator will need to approve (whitelist) these URLs in order for them to be accessible to your notebook once it is a deployed tool. Be sure to explain this in your ticket, and clearly identify the tool name and the reason each URL is needed.

To stop testing, close the browser session running inside your Workspace10, then type "control-c" in the terminal where you called the invoke script. Once the prompt returns, your notebook kernel has stopped.

You can make any adjustments needed to the underlying code before you flag your tool as Uploaded and continue with the deployment process.

title: Using Python packages from Jupyter Notebooks
content:
Using Python packages from Jupyter Notebooks

The Jupyter tool is a useful place to develop Python, R, or Octave code and analyses in a notebook style. Hub users can easily share their notebooks with other users by publishing notebooks as tools. A published Jupyter notebook enables other users to interact with the notebook, stepping through its cells and even changing them. When users run your published notebook, any changes they make to it will not persist.

Here we assume you are running: anaconda-7; debian10 container.

Python packages

Python has been extended to work with hundreds of specialized packages. For example, see the Anaconda package repo. A number of scientific Python packages are installed and accessible on the hub.

The hub uses Jupyter kernels to safely load needed Python packages. You can select a Jupyter kernel to set paths to a self-contained installation of specified packages, making them available in your notebook. This page will show you how to set access to Python packages from Jupyter Notebooks.

Note that we must install packages on the hub to make them available as a kernel. Submit a ticket to request new packages or a new kernel. 

Selecting a kernel

New notebook

To select the kernel for a new notebook, start a Jupyter tool. In the upper right, select 'New', then the kernel you want from the kernel menu. You can now import and use the kernel's packages in your notebook.

Be sure to save the notebook after changing the kernel.

Existing notebook

If you need to change the kernel for an existing notebook, first open the notebook in a Jupyter tool.

  1. If the notebook is already running, you must first shut it down by selecting Kernel: Shutdown from the menus.
  2. Then, you can select the kernel of your choice using the menu Kernel: Change Kernel: somekernel. After you have made the selection, check the displayed kernel name on the upper right of the notebook. It should match what you just selected.
  3. Finally, save the notebook, and your kernel choice will be saved along with it.

Kernel availability

How do we know what packages are available in what kernels?

  1. Check the conda env specification file associated with the kernel. 
  2. Run conda commands to interrogate the packages. Read the next section for further information.
Using conda to list installed packages

The kernels we have created to support different sets of Python packages are based on conda environments ("envs"). You can interrogate these conda envs to list the packages a given kernel supports. This is general to Anaconda package manager (more is available here). Below are a few tips.

Note that creating a conda env is an administrator action. If you need a new env or additional packages, enter a ticket to request them.

Example

The kernel named modgrnld-python3 contains the following packages and their dependencies:

  • matplotlib
  • rasterio
  • georaster
  • hublib
  • python 3.7
  • netCDF4
  • numpy
  • pyproj
  • scipy

What envs are available?

To access a conda env, first start a Workspace10 tool. On the command line, type the following command to set the anaconda installation in your path:

use anaconda-7

Now, to show the names of available envs:

conda info --envs

Note that we may not have created kernels for all the available envs.

What packages are in this env?

If you have an env enabled currently, to list packages there, type:

conda list

Or for an arbitrary env, someenv:

conda list -n <someenv>

Export current conda env

To export a list of the packages and versions installed in the env to a text-based .yml file:

conda activate <envname>
conda env export > <filename>.yml

title: Jupyter Tool Deployment Styles
content:
Jupyter tool deployment styles

How do you want your Jupyter Notebook-based tool to behave when a user runs it? You have several choices, which we describe here:

  1. Tool or App Mode style--code cells are hidden, UI widgets are visible
  2. Notebook style--all code cells are shown.  This is the default.

If you're working out how to develop and deploy the notebook, please refer to the other articles in this series. Continue reading to choose and set the tool display style.

Setting App Mode

You can achieve the dashboard-style effects by just selecting the App Mode in the Jupyter menu bar. Toggle back to edit your notebook using the Edit App button.

This screenshot shows the Jupyter tool menu bar, with its Appmode button

Deploying as App Mode

Then, to deploy the tool in App Mode, specify an -A in your invoke script, as follows:

/usr/bin/invoke_app "$@" -t toolname \
                         -C "start_jupyter -A -T @tool MyNotebook.ipynb" \
	                 -u anaconda-X \
                         -w headless \
                         -r none

The tool user will still be able to toggle the tool to show its code cells.  To suppress that behavior, add a -t to the start_jupyter call.

/usr/bin/invoke_app "$@" -t toolname \
                         -C "start_jupyter -A -t -T @tool MyNotebook.ipynb" \
	                 -u anaconda-X \
                         -w headless \
                         -r none

title: Tool Repository Structure
content:
The directory structure for tool repositories should start from the following:

      toolname/
         bin/
            .keep
         data/
            .keep
         doc/
            .keep
         examples/
            .keep
         middleware/
            invoke
         rappture/
            .keep
         simtool/
            TOOLNAME.ipynb
         src/
            Makefile

The .keep files are present to force git to track initially empty directories. Should the directories become populated the .keep file can be removed.  The simtool directory should be present only if the tool was registered with the publication option = Sim2L.  The rappture directory is only required for tools actually using Rappture.  The src directory should contain any source code that needs to be compiled and a Makefile to direct building of executables.  The Makefile must have the install, clean, and distclean targets. The bin directory should contain any executables created by issuing the make install command in the src directory.  The bin directory is automatically added to the PATH environment variable used to search for executable files.  It is common practice to put Jupyter notebook files in either the top level or bin directories.  It is also permissible to create additional directories as deemed necessary.

Invoke script template

All tools require that the executable file middleware/invoke be present.  The specifics of the invoke file depend on the tool publication classification.   Templates for the three categories of tools are shown here.  For tools where the repository is maintained on the HUB known values such as tool name are substituted in the template to provide an initial invoke file.

Sim2L

#!/bin/sh

#
# Sim2L
#
/usr/bin/invoke_app "$@" -t @TOOLNAME@ \
                         -C "start_jupyter -T @tool -t @TOOLNAME@Example.ipynb" \
                         -u anaconda-X \
                         -r none \
                         -w headless

Jupyter Notebook

#!/bin/sh

#
# jupyter tool
#
/usr/bin/invoke_app "$@" -t @TOOLNAME@ \
                         -C "start_jupyter -T @tool -t @TOOLNAME@.ipynb" \
                         -u anaconda-X \
                         -r none \
                         -w headless

Rappture/Linux GUI

#!/bin/sh

#
# standard tool
#
/usr/bin/invoke_app "$@" -t @TOOLNAME@ \
                         -C rappture

title: Secure Programming
content:
Software security flaws can be introduced at  any stage of the software development lifecycle, including:   

  • Not identifying security requirements up front
  • Creating conceptual designs that have logic errors
  • Using poor coding practices that introduce technical vulnerabilities
  • Deploying the software improperly  
  • Introducing flaws during maintenance or updating

Security by Design

Security needs to be a priority as you develop code, not an afterthought. Organizations may have competing priorities where software engineering and coding are concerned. Optimizing for security can conflict with optimizing for development speed. However, a “security by design” approach that puts security first tends to pay off in the long run, reducing the future cost of technical debt and risk mitigation. An analysis of your source code should be conducted throughout your SDLC, and security automation  implemented.  Both are in place.

Password Management

  • Store passwords and credentials only is specified locations by the Hubzero Security Officer.
  • Protect passwords and credentials per the policy and procedures for the credentials storage system.
  • Never save a password, key, or other credential in a code repository.

Access Control

Take a “default deny” approach to sensitive data. Limit privileges and restrict access to secure data to only users who need it. Deny access to any user that cannot demonstrate authorization. Ensure that requests for sensitive information are checked to verify that the user is authorized to access it. 

Error Handling and Logging

Software errors are often indicative of bugs, many of which cause vulnerabilities. Error handling and logging are two of the most useful techniques for minimizing their impact. Error handling attempts to catch errors in the code before they result in a catastrophic failure. Logging documents errors so that developers can diagnose and mitigate their cause. 

Documentation and logging of all failures, exceptions, and errors should be implemented on a trusted system to comply with secure coding standards.

For example, could there be an error that would return an empty page or make Apache send HTTP code 200?

Threat Modeling

Document, locate, address, and validate are the four steps to threat modeling. To securely code, you need to examine your software for areas susceptible to increased threats of attack. Threat modeling is a multi-stage process that should be integrated into the software lifecycle from development, testing, and production. 

Cryptographic Practices

Using quality modern cryptographic algorithms with keys stored in secure key vaults is a practice that increases the security of your code in the event of a breach.

Input Validation and Output Encoding

These secure coding standards are self-explanatory in that you need to identify all data inputs and sources and validate those classified as untrusted. You should utilize a standard routine for output encoding and input validation. Don't assume that because you set a value, e.g., in a "hidden input", it is still safe to use after going through the client browser! In other words, can you absolutely guarantee that a variable is safe to use?  If not, systematically verify it with input validation.

Adopt a secure coding standard.

Develop and apply a secure coding standard for your target development language and platform.

Use effective quality assurance techniques.

Good quality assurance techniques can be effective in identifying and eliminating vulnerabilities. Fuzz testing, penetration testing, and source code audits should all be incorporated as part of an effective quality assurance program. Independent security reviews can lead to more secure systems.


Check the OWASP top ten issues

Verify that your web application code won't be vulnerable to any of the issues described at https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/

Reference Guide

A reference guide https://owasp.org/www-pdf-archive/OWASP_Code_Review_Guide_v2.pdf

title: Metadata and Privacy
content:
The Metadata Information Leakage Problem

Vulnerability scanners report the presence of metadata in images served by web servers.  This includes several types of metadata, such as Exif, which can reveal dates, GPS coordinates, and more, which are details that may not have been indended to be published, and may have consequences similar to "doxing".

Hubs have a more complicated situation than a basic web site because they contain and republish data;  the metadata may matter and even be part of the scientific value of the data and publications that a hub curates. Data creators and owners are best positioned to identify which metadata has value, and which present privacy risks. Hubs are typically curators without the information and manpower necessary to make decisions about the metadata. Therefore, the metadata must be filtered before being uploaded. To bring awareness of this issue, hubs shall include by default the following sentences in their published privacy policy:

"Users are responsible for any privacy issues consequent to uploading files containing metadata (e.g., images with GPS coordinates). Users are responsible for stripping metadata, as appropriate, before uploading files."

title: Ansible for Configuration Management, Provisioning and Disaster Recovery
content:
The Ansible playbooks and roles used by SDSC HUBzero apply to the SDSC RDS, SDSC Sherlock, and AWS environments.  We use Ansible playbooks to provision systems and manage their configurations.  We also use Ansible to update the HUBzero CMS code, for which there is a separate documentation page.  We recommend running Ansible as a way of detecting and fixing configuration issues, and during disaster recovery when applicable, e.g., to provision new VMs.  Do not make manual changes to hosts;  all changes should be done through Ansible, so that during Disaster Recovery, a host can be completely rebuilt by running the appropriate Ansible playbooks.

Getting Started

To start using Ansible, get a copy of the Ansible repository:

git clone git@gitlab.com:sdsc-rds/systems/hubzero-ansible.git

Note that there are 2 inventories of hosts, one for production (inventories/prod_hosts.ini) and one for non-production (inventories/non_prod_hosts.ini).  Make sure to use the right inventory for the host's status (use the "-i" option for the "ansible-playbook" command). 

Provisioning

Provisioning is done by running the appropriate playbook for the host type.  To setup a "web server without tools" for the first time:

  • Make sure the hostname is in the "only_web" group in the inventory
  • Run playbooks/hubzero.only_web.new_install.yml
  • Run playbooks/hubzero.only_web.maint.yml

To setup a web server with tools, first set it up as a webserver without tools as above, then:

  • In the inventory, move the hostname from the "only_web" group to the "web_with_tools" group
  • Run playbooks/hubzero.web_with_tools.new_install.yml
  • Run playbooks/hubzero.web_with_tools.maint.yml

To setup an execution host:

  • Make sure the hostname is in the "exec" group in the inventory
  • Run playbooks/hubzero.exechost.maint.yml

Configuration Management

Run the playbooks with ".maint" in their name, for the appropriate host type.  It is fine to run separately the roles that apply.

Disaster Recovery and Upgrades to new VMs

Running the above playbooks works for new hubs and existing hubs.  However, during disaster recovery or even procedures like Operating System upgrades, the data from an old VM may need to be migrated to a new VM.  In that case, the storage from the old VMs, or a backup image in the case of disaster recovery, can be mounted at /mnt on the new VM.  The playbook "playbooks/hubzero.copy_data_webservers_upgrade.yml" will migrate the data from the /mnt mounts to the new storage locations in the new VM.

title: SDSC RDS Hub Decommission
content:
Hubzero

  • Schedule decommission date with client.  Wait for date to be scheduled.  Continue on the scheduled date.  Clients should copy their data or make a list of data we need to copy for them.
  • In PRTG, move hosts and service IPs to the “non-prod” group.  (may submit a ticket to RDS specifically for this, wait until complete to continue).
  • Move hosts to nonprod inventory in Ansible, and rename the group_vars file from “prod_hubname” to “nonprod_hubname”.  Use “grep” to make sure that inventories/prod_hosts.ini has no references left to the hub.
  • In Ansible inventory, remove the “prod_hubname” group from the production inventory file and merge it with the “nonprod_hubname” group in the nonprod inventory.  Example:
    • [hubname:children]
    • nonprod_hubname
    • [nonprod_hubname]
      • web01.int.hubname.org
      • exec01.hubname.org
      • stage.hubname.org
  • In the host_vars file for the webserver, set “decommissioned: true”.
  • Run the appropriate Ansible maintenance playbook “hubzero.only_web.maint.yml” to restrict web and SSH access to the hub hosts to behind the UCSD firewall.  If the maintenance playbook fails for some reason, at least run the hubzero.iptables role.
  • Copy docker images from an execution host to the webhost for final backup.  (Execution hosts will not have a final backup created).
  • Perform data exports and archived backups for hub owners via provided script. The full procedure is described in the script (https://gitlab.hubzero.org/hubzero/hub_backup_script ).
  • Decommission can proceed when backups for clients have been provided on help.hubzero.org, we do not need to wait for them to pick them up to continue.
  • Client backups will be available for 1 month.  Storage on help.hubzero.org can be expanded temporarily for client pickup via USS.
  • Submit a support ticket to RDS to complete the decommission procedure below (specifically list all hosts).


RDS

  • Perform full backup (VM snapshot) of all hub hosts specified except for execution hosts.
  • This backup should be retained for 1 year from the date of decommission.
  • Other backups may be removed.
  • Remove VMs from PRTG.
  • Shut down the VMs associated with the decommissioning hub.
  • Remove VMs from Ansible inventory (host vars, group var, non_prod_hosts file).  Commit changes back to the Ansible repository.
  • Update network firewall.
  • Release subnet and reclaim IPs.
  • Add a note to the support ticket with billing updates, if applicable.
  • Add a note to the support ticket that the decommission procedure is complete and close the ticket.

title: Database Accounts Policy
content:
Host Wildcards

The use of wildcards to specify the allowed sources of connections is strongly discouraged (e.g., in the mysql.user.host column). The main CMS account MUST NOT allow host wildcards for any reason, as this account is authoritative for almost all user accounts, group membership and authentication.

Remote Access to Database Accounts

Direct remote access to a MySQL account requires SSL to protect the connection, unless the account provides only read access to public data.  The MySQL account is protected by setting mysql.user.ssl_type to a value like “ANY”. 

MySQL Accounts for people

User grants to a hub's database MUST NOT allow access to the password hashes of other users unless required, and even then it must be approved by the HUBzero ISO.

Views

Use “SQL SECURITY INVOKER” instead of “SQL SECURITY DEFINER” in view creation statements. Otherwise, views need to be dropped and recreated when changing user access permissions. With SQL SECURITY DEFINER, you will get a warning/error if the combo user@host does not exist, every time you access the view.

title: Create a read-only MySQL account
content:
Make sure you read the policy on database accounts before creating accounts.

This procedure has been used on db2.nanohub.org to create a read-only account.  Similar steps can be taken on hubs as well.  Besides being read-only, the privilege grants are designed to prevent reading password hashes.

 

1. Generate a 16-character alphanumeric random password, without special characters

2. Create the account in MySQL

GRANT USAGE ON *.* TO '<username>_ro'@'localhost' identified by '<random password>';

3. Generate an SQL file with the correct grant commands
Enter this multiline command in MySQL, substituting the correct username:

SELECT CONCAT("GRANT SELECT ON nanohub.", table_name, " TO <username>_ro@localhost;")
FROM information_schema.TABLES
WHERE table_schema = "nanohub" AND table_name <> "jos_xprofiles" AND table_name <> "jos_users" AND table_name <> "jos_users" AND table_name <> "jos_users_password" AND table_name <> "jos_users_password_history"  AND table_name <> "jos_xprofiles2" INTO OUTFILE '/var/log/mysql_backups/grants_ro';

4. Load the SQL file into MySQL

grep -v '-' /var/log/mysql_backups/grants_ro | sed 's/|//g' | mysql

5. Additional grant commands
In MySQL, enter the following commands, substituting the correct username:

GRANT SELECT (id, name, username, email, usertype, block, approved, sendEmail,registerDate, lastvisitDate, activation, params, lastResetTime, resetCount) ON nanohub.jos_users TO '<username>_ro'@'localhost';

GRANT SELECT (uidNumber,name , username, email, registerDate, gidNumber, homeDirectory, loginShell, ftpShell, gid, orgtype, organization, countryresident, countryorigin, gender, url, reason, mailPreferenceOption, usageAgreement, modifiedDate, emailConfirmed, regIP, regHost, nativeTribe, phone,proxyUidNumber , givenName, middleName, surname, picture, vip, public, params, note, shadowExpire, locked, orcid) ON nanohub.jos_xprofiles TO '<username>_ro'@'localhost';

flush privileges;

6. Communicate the password to the new user via a secure channel, e.g., write it in a file in the home directory and suggest deleting the file

 

Variant Procedure

This variant procedure solved Ticket #11107 on help.hubzero.org:

Please grant read-only database access on prod communityhub.purdue.edu for usernames "rhine,apsheetz,jgmyers,bmccart,biehl" for tables jos_cart*, jos_storefront*, and jos_users.id, jos_users.name,jos_users.username,jos_users.email, jos_users.lastvisitDate fields only.

We're going to create a new MySQL user account for each, and store the password in /tmp.  Steps to the solution:

  • Create a random password for each new MySQL account
  • Create the MySQL account
  • Grant permissions on the required tables and columns
rand_alnum () {
  openssl rand -base64 15 | sed 's/[^a-zA-Z0-9]//g' | cut -c1-16
}
umask 077
# rhine
for u in  apsheetz jgmyers bmccart biehl; do
  muser=${u}_mysql
  new_pass=`rand_alnum`
  mysql -e "GRANT USAGE ON *.* TO '$muser'@'localhost' identified by '$new_pass'"
  echo "$new_pass" > /tmp/${u}.mysql.pass
  chown ${u} /tmp/${u}.mysql.pass
  for t in `mysql -B --skip-column-names -e "show tables like 'jos_storefront%'" pch`; do
    mysql -e "GRANT SELECT ON pch.$t TO '$muser'@'localhost'"
  done
  for t in `mysql -B --skip-column-names -e "show tables like 'jos_cart%'" pch`; do
     mysql -e "GRANT SELECT ON pch.$t TO '$muser'@'localhost'"
  done
  mysql -e "GRANT SELECT (id, name, username, email, lastvisitDate) ON pch.jos_users TO '$muser'@'localhost'"
  mysql -e "show grants for '$muser'@'localhost'"
done  
mysql -e "flush privileges"

title: Information Access Management
content:
Goal

Implement policies and procedures for authorizing access to electronic protected health information that are consistent with the applicable requirements of subpart E of this part.

Definition

Privileged access to a HUBzero science gateway deployment is defined as having physical access to the underlying hardware, or administrative access to the virtualization layer, or any access to the "/administrator" pages of the web service, or any privilege on the operating system and the services it runs that exceeds that given automatically to people registering for an account on the science gateway using the interface provided to do so.  Examples of this are “superuser” access to the "/administrator" pages of the web service, root access to some layer of the infrastructure, being a member of an “access-” group (see role-based access controls for an explanation of the “access-” groups), or any combination of privileges allowing one to act as an account running an important service, or root. In effect, this privileged access either outright grants access to EPHI information, or potentially makes it easier to abuse flaws.

Access Authorization

a. Procedure for permitting access to EPHI.

The person granting privileged access must verify that the workforce member needs this access.

The person granting privileged access to a HIPAA-covered system must verify that the workforce member has taken appropriate HIPAA training.  This training shall satisfy the requirements of any parent organization under which HUBzero operates.

All hub user (CMS) account information is stored in LDAP and MySQL. Local user accounts can be used for administrators of the operating system that do not have hub accounts, or for development systems that do not handle HIPAA data. Otherwise, local accounts for people on HUBzero infrastructure systems must be kept to a minimum and their use must be justified, especially if this access may grant access to EPHI information.

The person granting privileged access must verify that any user’s mobile devices that will be used with HIPAA-covered hubs comply with the encryption policy (see “164.312 Technical Safeguards a Access Control”).

System accounts, that is, accounts used for running a system service or some other function such as running automated scripts, must not be associated with a particular person, and must not be used for login purposes by people.

b. Procedure for logging and tracking authorization of access to EPHI.

Tracking authorization of access to EPHI is done by gathering the list of users with established privileged access, as defined above. In other words, HUBzero uses the establishment of privileged access as a record of authorization.

c. Procedure for reviewing and revising, on a periodic basis, authorization of access to EPHI.

Every year, an audit will verify if workforce members that were authorized, have done or refreshed the required HIPAA training. Twice a year an audit will verify that they still need this access. Local accounts on HUBzero infrastructure which may grant access to EPHI information will also be reviewed.


Access Establishment and Modification


1. Process for establishing, documenting, reviewing, and modifying access to EPHI

a. Procedure for establishing and documenting access to EPHI.

This is done by granting privileged access as defined above, by the appropriate mechanism. Accesses to EPHI are not documented by HUBzero, and are the responsibility of the covered application or service hosted by SDSC HUBzero.

b. Procedure for documenting establishment of access to EPHI.

The establishment of access to EPHI, by itself, is not documented separately by HUBzero.

c. Procedure for reviewing on a regular basis workforce members’ access privileges to EPHI.

Every year, a list of which workforce members that have privileged access to systems with EPHI information will be made, both through local or central accounts. Authorization will then be verified, and access privileges modified accordingly.

d. Procedure for modifying the access privileges of workforce members to EPHI, as appropriate, based on the periodic reviews.

This is done by using the mechanism by which privileged access was granted, as described above.

2. Authorization and training of workforce members to access EPHI


a. Definition and classification of permitted access methods

Workforce members must use encrypted communication protocols (e.g., SSH) to access the systems and services for which they have privileged access. Clear text protocols (e.g., MySQL, telnet) are expressly forbidden. Workforce members will be shown how to use SSH for tunneling clear text protocols, therefore encrypting the communication.

b. Definition and classification of length of time access will be permitted.

Access will be permitted until a workforce member changes positions or an audit determines that their privileged access is not needed anymore.

c. Procedure for appropriate logging and tracking of activities by an authorized workforce member on EPHI.

Activities of workforce members with privileged access are tracked the same on all HUBzero infrastructure regardless of whether EPHI is involved. HUBzero tracks logins via SSH and the web server.

 

Previous versions of this policy are available in the old wiki at https://help.hubzero.org/groups/hubzero_hipaa/wiki/164308a4InformationAccessManagement

title: Change Management Procedures
content:
Purpose

The purpose of these procedures is to minimize the risk and impact of changes to systems managed by HUBzero and its subcontractors, and make sure related information is shared and communicated appropriately. For purposes of this procedure, a change is defined as anything that transforms, alters, or modifies the operating environment.  For this purpose, the security impacts of changes must be analyzed prior to change implementation.

Definitions

The roles used in this document, and their responsibilities, are described in the HUBzero Incident Response Plan.

Regular Maintenance

No change request is used for scheduled regular routine maintenance, such as patching software, or mandated periodic processes carried on by authorized personel, such as the review of account privileges, which can explicitly result in the revocation of privileges.  That’s because the mandate to perform these tasks is equivalent to approved, standing change requests.

Version Control Repositories

Version control systems, e.g., git, must be used to record changes made to code and Ansible roles and variables, so changes can be re-examined or reversed if any problems are discovered later, and for historical purposes.  Configuration changes to production systems must always be made through Ansible or git code repositories and never directly to the systems with manual changes, to avoid the reversal of manual changes, to make sure that systems can be reconfigured exactly the same way, and to make sure that Ansible and git code repositories are sufficient to describe the state and baseline of all configuration items.  This does not apply to configuration items using the "/administrator" URL of a hub for technical reasons.

Code Changes

All code changes to the "HUBzero CMS", which is stored in the git repository named "hubzero-cms", currently at https://github.com/hubzero/hubzero-cms, are subject to code reviews.  Code reviews are recommended, but not required, for other HUBzero software.

Code reviews must include consideration of the potential security impacts of code changes.  For this purpose, participants in code reviews should include someone trained in secure programming techniques.

CMS Administrator Configuration Changes

Changes to configuration items using the "/administrator" URL of a hub must have been requested by a hub owner, or must be accepted by the hub owners if they will result in changes to the "user experience", defined as system-wide changes visible, or noticeable to users of a HUB by a change of behavior.  For example, changes to password strength and expiration rules must be accepted.  Furthermore, changes to FISMA-certified hubs must be analyzed for potential security impacts by the HUBzero ISO or a designated security analyst.

Changes to or touching security features

After implementation of a change to security features, or a change that touched something used by security features (e.g., a dependency), the related security features shall be tested for correct functionality.  If the change was tracked with a "Trello" card, the card must be labeled "security" and have a checklist added describing the tests to be performed.  Those tests must be completed before the Trello card is moved out of the "In Progress" column.

New Services

Requests for new behaviors and services, etc., MUST be requested via tickets or Trello cards to provide logs and historical records. Change requests via emails, chat, or walk-ins will not be accepted unless a ticket is also filed or a Trello card is created.  When a VIP sends an email requesting changes, the appropriate response for the recipient staff would be to create a ticket or a Trello card on behalf of the VIP, or request a ticket, depending on the situation, assuming the ticketing system is available.

Changes initiated by system administrators MUST be communicated to communication managers if they are likely to or will result in service outages of more than a few seconds.

All changes to FISMA-certified hubs must be analyzed for potential security impacts by the HUBzero ISO or a designated security analyst.

Configuration changes initiated by system administrators that could modify communications received by client browsers or subsystems managed by CMS administrators, MUST be reviewed by CMS administrators before deployment in production. This review will be initiated by a request for review, stating the nature of the change and expected impact, as well as a date by which the review is desired to be done, and a deployment plan. The request can be emailed or transmitted via other means deemed appropriate.  CMS administrators can request discussions in meetings or additional delays for research and testing, as needed, and as circumstances require.

CMS administrators are encouraged to approve security-related changes early for HIPAA-covered hubs, at greater operational risk, due to an increased aversion to security risks. Different outcomes may be desirable for different types of hubs. Communication managers will also be notified at the same time and can veto or delay a change for specific hubs. Communication managers can request additional explanations and meetings with hub stakeholders to discuss the changes.  In all cases, the security impacts of approving, delaying, or rejecting the changes must be taken into account.

Support Requests and Trouble Reports

Inquiries about an error, malfunction or deviations from previously specified behavior SHOULD be reported and resolved via tickets. Reports via emails, chat, or walk-ins will be discouraged, but accepted on a best-effort attempt basis with the expectation that a ticket will be filed. Trivial changes made in response (e.g., tweaking a user’s disk quota) do not need to be logged or communicated. Changes of a greater scale (i.e., systematic changes affecting several HUBs) MUST be communicated if they might result in a noticeable service interruption or in noticeable side effects.

Emergency Work

In case a major problem is detected (e.g., hardware failure, complete outage of a major service), the Incident Response Plan (IRP) should be consulted, with possible escalation to the Disaster Recovery and Business Continuity Plan.  The IRP includes "Communication Guidelines", describing who should communicate what and when.  Additionally, system administrators SHOULD communicate to communication managers that they are aware of a problem and working on it. During emergencies, review processes described in the above sections will not be followed. For this purpose, emergencies are defined as serious threats to the integrity of hubs or to the confidentiality of HIPAA data;  for example, evidence of attempts to compromise a vulnerable service.

title: Sherlock Change Request Form
content:
The Request for Change email format below is intended to provide an easy to understand tag or bullet approach to convey critical information, to set expectations and to convey urgency or lack thereof for the requested change.

 

A new email should be written and configured to include all of the following and at least one option from each:

TO field.

CC field.

A tag of [Issue] or [Request].  ** [Issue] is to be used when requesting a change to resolve an issue. [Request] is to be used for all other requests.

A tag of [Dev], [Stage] or  [Prod].  ** Refers to a development, staging or production host environment.

A tag of [Work Impaired: Unknown],[Work Impaired: Yes], or [Work Impaired: No].  ** Refers to whether or not an end-uses, client, or staff member's work is directly impacted by what is needed in the request.

A tag of [Requested Max Resolution: "time_frame" ] ** "time_frame" should be an integer of days or weeks and refers to the time to completion that may be needed.

A tag of [Impact:  "impact_description"].  ** "impact_description" is a description that provides a sense or urgency or lack thereof for the request on a user or group of users.
