title: Jupyter Notebooks
content:
Adding additional packages to Jupyter Notebooks

Google the desired package (python, R packages, not OS packages) and review the installation instructions.  They might recommend a different conda repository than the default.
Be careful if conda says it wants to downgrade packages.  If it is a minor downgrade, it is probably OK.  Do not proceed if many packages must be downgraded or critical packages are to be downgraded.  Remember that changes to the Ananconda environment will affect all tools using the environment and a downgrade could cause tools not to function (if a feature is no longer available, for example).

  • Start a workspace tool.  If your HUB supports multiple operating system (vendor or version) based tool containers choose the workspace tool for the appropriate container.
  • As an alternative, start the Jupyter Notebook tool based on the Anaconda environment that you want to modify and start a new terminal.
  • From the open terminal switch to the apps user (your account must be a member of the apps group). 
    • sudo su - apps
  • Load the Anaconda environment that you wish to modify (there may be multiple Anaconda environments available.  The list of Anaconda environments can be listed with the command 
    • use |& grep anaconda
  • Execute the command "use", choosing the appropriate Anaconda (X represents the particular version choice) environment. 
    • use -e -r anaconda-X
  • Install the desired package via conda or mamba if it is installed.  mamba is typically much more efficient and provides more useful information should it fail.   Another option is to use pip.  Extra care must be taken when mixing conda and pip package installations in the same environment.  Typical installation command like 
    • conda install -c conda-forge -c defaults <pkgname>
    • pip install -U --upgrade-strategy only-if-needed <pkgname>
    The installation may take a few minutes
  • Important! Fix any world writable files by doing: 
    • chmod -R o-w /apps/share64/<OS>/anaconda/anaconda-X

Creating a separate anaconda environment.

In some circumstances it is beneficial to spawn a new named environment from the standard base environment.  The named environments are referred to as kernels in Jupyter notebooks.  Once a Jupyter notebook is running the developer or user has the opportunity to change to a different kernel.  The kernel used to run the notebook is embedded within the notebook metadata therefore only has to be changed once.  This works well for developers and means the administrator does not have to create a Jupyter Notebook tool for each kernel.

  • Set base Anaconda environment 
    • use -e -r anaconda-X
  • Create new named environment 
    • conda create -n <name>
  • Activate named environment 
    • source activate <name>
  • Do package installation as before 
    • conda install -c conda-forge -c defaults <pkgname>
    • pip install -U --upgrade-strategy only-if-needed <pkgname>
  • Register named environment as kernel in base environment 
    • python -m ipykernel install --sys-prefix --name <name> --display-name "Python3 (<name>)"
    • python -m ipykernel install --prefix /apps/share64/<OS>/anaconda/anaconda-X --name <name> --display-name "Python3 (<name>)"
  • Deactivate named environment 
    • conda deactivate

 

References:

conda user guide

Ipython kernel instalation

 

Updating hublib

The HUBzero utility library should be installed in every base Anaconda environment and in each named environment as well.  The hublib package is available only through pip.

  • Set Anaconda base environment 
    • use -e -r anaconda-X
  • Install hublib 
    • pip install -U hublib

title: Installing Tool Dependencies
content:
Occasionally additional software needs to be installed in a tool environment to support tool execution.  Please follow these instructions in the given order.  Keep in mind that an environment maybe shared by multiple tools.

 

Install a operating system package in the tool execution container

Tool execution containers are based on Docker images.  At minimum Debian 7 (wheezy) and Debian 10 (buster) Docker images are provided.   Operating system choice is not limited to Debian.  We have used CentOS and Ubuntu images as the basis for images to meet tool requirements.   Regardless of operating system choice there is a minimum set of scripts and configuration files that must be included to enable the middleware to manage container related processes.

The pairing of Docker image and tool is made according to the following convention:

  1. Find an image tag matching tool name and revision.
  2. Find an image tag matching the tool name.
  3. A default image specified in the middleware.

Multiple Docker tags may be applied to the same image thus reducing the storage requirement for multiple images.  Docker images may be modified or created using standard practices based on Dockerfiles.  If all Docker images are not made available on all execution hosts, host requirements may be used to aid in execution host selection.

Manually install software in the 'use' infrastructure

Typically we create and run Hapi (HUBzero Apps Program Installers) scripts to download, configure, compile, and install software in the tool execution environment.  This is especially important when multiple versions of the same software must be available to server different tools. For example, Tool A may require R version 3.6.3 while Tool B may require R version 4.2.1.  These requirements are the result of an ever evolving software landscape.   "Use" is very helpful in this case, among others, providing a way to load specific software versions as requirements demand.

All operations for manually installing dependent software for tools must be done by the apps user from a workspace terminal.

As the apps user clone the Hapi repo into the apps home directory:

git clone https://github.com/hubzero/hapi.git

In the hapi/scripts directory you will find a collection of shell scripts and csv files for software typically installed for use in tool environments.  If a script exists for software that you need, just run it!  Feel free to add new Hapi scripts of your creation to the GitHub repo by submitting pull requests.  We occasionally add scripts as well.

If, after doing a git update on your repository, a script doesn't exist for the software you need, copy an existing Hapi script and modify it.  Hapi scripts make your life much easier by downloading, configuring, compiling, installing and even adding the required 'use' environ.d file to the appropriate location.

All tool dependencies are installed by the apps user in an operating system specific directory such as  /apps/share64/debian7 and should be owned by the apps user and group.  All files must be readable by everyone and all directories must be searchable by everyone.  No files or directories should be writable by everyone ( seriously don't do this )

* For a full manual run "man use" from a tool session terminal.

 

USE(1)                           User Commands                          USE(1)

NAME
       use, unuse - adjust the shell environment

SYNOPSIS
       use [options]... [ENVIRONMENT]
       unuse [options]... [ENVIRONMENT]

DESCRIPTION
       The  use  command incorporates the specified ENVIRONMENT to the current
       shell.  The unuse command removes it.  It optionally records the selec-
       tion  persistently  so that subsequent shells will use the ENVIRONMENT.
       These commands are independent of the shell being run.

       An ENVIRONMENT is specified by a configuration file of the same name as
       found in one of the configuration directories.  The ENVIRON_CONFIG_DIRS
       environment variable specifies a list of directories in which to search
       for  configurations.   Each configured ENVIRONMENT specifies a environ-
       ment variables to set or prepend, shell variables  to  set,  and  shell
       aliases to set.

       Some environments are configured to conflict with others.  The use com-
       mand will ask if conflicting ENVIRONMENT should be replaced.

       With no arguments, the use and unuse commands will print a synopsys  of
       options and lists all available environments.

       -h     print available help for a named ENVIRONMENT.

       -e     environment only.  Do not ask about preserving the selection.

       -p     modify the environment and preserve selection.  Do not ask about
              preserving the selection.

       -k     keep any conflicting environment.  Do not  ask  about  replacing
              it.

       -r     replace any conflicting environment without asking.

       -x     quietly  ignore  the  command if the named ENVIRONMENT cannot be
              found.

MAKING IT WORK
       The following command will describe an environment named xyz:

              use -h xyz

       The following command will incorporate the xyz  environment  preserving
       the  environment  for future shell invocations.  It will also not over-
       ride any conflicting environments:

              use -p -k xyz

       The following command will remove the xyz environment  but  retain  its
       use for future sessions:

              unuse -e xyz

INTERNAL OPERATION
       use  and  unuse  are  actually  implemented  as  shell functions (or as
       aliases in the case of csh  derivatives).   The  functions  pass  their
       arguments to the /etc/environ script which determines the commands that
       the shell should execute to satisfy the new environment  configuration.
       The  script prints these commands, the shell function receives them and
       evals them.

ENVIRONMENT CONFIGURATION FILES
       Configuration files are interpreted shell scripts.  Several  predefined
       functions are available to make the the process automatic.

       alias NAME "Replacement"
              Set a command alias in the shell.

       conflict VARNAME
              Define  an  environment  variable  to indicate that a type of an
              ENVIRONMENT is in use.  All conflicting  ENVIRONMENT  configura-
              tions should specify the same conflict.  An ENVIRONMENT configu-
              ration may specify multiple conflicts.

       desc "A short description..."
              A short description of the ENVIRONMENT.

       help "A lengthy description..."
              A long description of the ENVIRONMENT and how to use  it.   This
              description will be formatted when printed.

       prepend VARNAME ADDITION
              Prepend  ADDITION  to the environment variable VARNAME separated
              with a colon.

       setenv VARNAME REPLACEMENT
              Set or replace the environment variable  VARNAME  with  REPLACE-
              MENT.

       shellset VARNAME REPLACEMENT
              Set or replace the shell variable VARNAME with REPLACEMENT.

title: DataCite
content:
DataCite MDS API Application 

The DataCite Metadata Store (MDS) API[1] is going to be used for Hub dataset Digital Identifier Object (DOI) and corresponding metadata creation and update. 

 

1. Introduction 

The DataCite Metadata Store (MDS) API is the default API for registering DataCite DOIs and associated metadata. Below shows the requirements for using the MDS API. 

(1) The API requires authentication. If your hub or university is member of DataCite and has DataCite credentials then you can configure DataCite to mint DOIs for your hub's publications and tools. DataCite also has a testing guide to help with troubleshooting.

(2) DataCite assigns the DOI prefix. 

(3) DOI request needs to transfer through HTTPS. 

(4) HTTP basic authentication is performed in the DataCite Metadata Store API usage. 

2. DOI register 

The DOI registration takes two steps, first is to register DOI metadata, and second is to register the DOI name and dataset URL. 

2.1 Registering DOI metadata 

The DOI metadata for dataset includes title, author, dates, description, and so on. All the metadata that a hub collects for a dataset shows in table 1. Metadata element 

Explanation 

Identifier 

Identifier type is doi, and the value of identifier is the doi. 

Creators/creator/creatorName 

Author(s) of the dataset 

nameIdentifier 

nameIdentifierScheme is ORCID， and value is the ORICID. 

titles/title 

Name of the dataset. 

publisher 

Holder of the dataset 

publicationYear 

The year when the dataset is published 

Contributors/contributor/contributorName 

Project leader's name 

dates 

There are two metadata elements, one is when dataType is Valid, the value is the date when the dataset is submitted on the hub; Another is when the datatype is Accepted, the value is the date when the dataset is approved for publish on the hub. 

language 

It is set to en by default 

resourceType 

resourceTypeGeneral is set to the resourceType designated by the hub. The value is the resourceTypeTitle. 

RelatedIdentifiers/relatedIdentifier 

relatedIdentifierType is DOI, relationType is IsNewVersionOf, and the value is the relatedDoi, which is DOI of the resource that reference this dataset. 

version 

Publication version 

rights 

The license that user selects in the dataset submission workflow on the hub 

Descriptions/description 

DescriptionType is Abstract, and the value is the abstract of the dataset 

 

The metadata elements in table 1 are saved in xml format as showing below. 

<resource xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns="http://datacite.org/schema/kernel-4" xsi:schemaLocation="http://datacite.org/schema/kernel-4 http://schema.datacite.org/meta/kernel-4.1/metadata.xsd"> 

<identifier identifierType="DOI">doi</identifier> 

<creators> 

<creator> 

<creatorName>name 1</creatorName> 

</creator> 

<creator> 

<creatorName>name 2</creatorName> 

</creator> 

<creator> 

<creatorName>name 3</creatorName> 

</creator> 

<creator> 

<creatorName>name 4</creatorName> 

<nameIdentifier nameIdentifierScheme="ORCID">orcid goes here</nameIdentifier> 

</creator> 

</creators> 

<titles> 

<title>title</title> 

</titles> 

<publisher>YOUR HUB's NAME</publisher> 

<publicationYear>year</publicationYear> 

<contributors> 

<contributor contributorType="ProjectLeader"> 

<contributorName>name</contributorName> 

</contributor> 

</contributors> 

<dates> 

<date dateType="Valid">date</date> 

<date dateType="Accepted">date</date> 

</dates> 

<language>en</language> 

<resourceType resourceTypeGeneral="Dataset">Datasets</resourceType> 

<version>1.0</version> 

<rights>Attribution 3.0 Unporte</rights> 

<descriptions> 

<description descriptionType="Abstract"> 

Description goes here 

</description> 

</descriptions> 

</resource> 

All the metadata elements conform to the DataCite metadata schema [2] standards. 

The MDS API can generate random DOI name when prefix is included in the metadata registration. The identifier in the metadata xml can be left empty in this case. 

The curl package can be used to submit the metadata to MDS service, see example below. Note that the [PREFIX] would need to be replaced with your hub's DataCite prefix. 

curl -H "Content-Type:application/xml;charset=UTF-8" -X PUT -i --user username:password -d @[PREFIX].xml https://mds.test.datacite.org/metadata/10.5072 

The response to the call above is OK ([PREFIX]/XXXX-XXXX). We need take the DOI out from there and use for further process. 

The identifier value in the metadata xml on DataCite will be replaced by the DOI name that is created in this step. 

The DOI is set to Draft state [3] after the metadata are registered. 

 

1.2.2 Registering the URL 

The second step is to register the DOI name and the URL that refers to the dataset. Below is an example of the curl command. Note that DOI name and URL to the dataset is included. 

curl -H "Content-Type:text/plain;charset=UTF-8" -X PUT --user username:password -d $'doi=[PREFIX]/0000-03VCnurl=http://example.org/publications/1' https://mds.test.datacite.org/doi/10.5072/0000-03VC 

The DOI transits from Draft state to Findable state after the DOI name and URL is registered. 

Below table includes the endpoint and other useful information that need to use in the DOI registration in production. The endpoint, prefix, username and password need to be configured on the admin interface for any development and production environments. 

Value 

DOI prefix 

[PREFIX]

MDS production endpoint 

https://mds.datacite.org 

 

2. Update DOI Metadata Records 

Update the DOI metadata is the same as storing a new version of the DOI metadata. According to the MDS API document, we need to issue a post of the metadata xml to DataCite. Below is an example on what the curl command should look like for such operation. 

$ curl -H "Content-Type: application/xml;charset=UTF-8" -X POST -i --user username:password -d @[PREFIX]/JQX3-61AT.xml https://mds.test.datacite.org/metadata 

 

Reference list 

1. https://support.datacite.org/docs/mds-api-guide 

2. http://schema.datacite.org/ 

3. https://support.datacite.org/docs/doi-states 

4. https://support.datacite.org/docs/testing-guide

 

 

 

Switching from EZID to DataCite

  1. Navigate to /administrator and login to the backend of the Hub
  2. Click on Components and then select Publications
  3. Click on Options and then click on DOI Configuration
    1. Note: You will only be able to access the Options button if you are a super user.
  4. Locate Enable DataCite or EZID DOI Service and select from the drop-down the appropriate option
    1. Note: When the "DataCite" is selected, the DataCite DOI service is activated and only DataCite related options on the configuration form are going to show up. When "EZID" is selected, EZID DOI service is activated and only EZID related options on the configuration form are going to show up. When "None" is selected, all options related to DOI service will be hidden. When users publish a dataset in this case, a message saying that "No DOI service is selected and please contact site administrator" is popping up.
  5. Click Save & Close

title: ITaP Data Center Security Policies and Procedures (Historical)
content:
ITaP Data Center

Security Policies and Procedures

 

1.0 Introduction

 

The security of the equipment and data in the ITaP Data Centers is vitally important to the daily functioning of Purdue University. Computer systems, networking and telecommunications hardware and software, and the data that is stored and transmitted must be protected and preserved.

 

The purpose of this document is to communicate the polices and procedures by which IT Infrastructure Operations and those customers who make use of the Data Center will maintain an appropriate level of security within the Data Center.

 

1.1 Provisions

 

  1. Data Centers will be protected from unauthorized access.

  2. Data Centers or ITaP facilities, which house sensitive or high-risk equipment, will be protected against fire, water, and other hazards.

  3. Devices that are critical to the operation of Purdue University business processes will be protected against power failure.

  4. Records will be kept (e.g. manual sign in sheets, door access logs, etc.) to track all staff and visitors accessing facilities and data centers.

  5. Reception areas will be designated to receive visitors to the facilities/data centers.

  6. Monitoring equipment/devices will be installed in data centers to monitor door access, environmental conditions (e.g. temperature, humidity, fire, smoke, water).

  7. Security awareness program will be instituted to educate staff as to proper security policies and procedures.

  8. Procedures will be developed for the secure disposal of computing equipment containing sensitive data.

  9. Incident Response Team (IRT) will be created and escalation procedures established.

  10. Business Impact Analysis (BIA) will be conducted on all systems, applications, and platforms.

  11. Security Risk Assessment will be completed to assess physical security at all facilities.

 

 

2.0 Policies

 

2.1 Access to an ITaP Data Center

 

  1. All personnel entering an ITaP Data Center must have proper authorization.

    1. Level I Authorization provides for access to data center after identity verification by Operations Staff.

    2. Level II Authorization provides for access to data center via card key access.

    3. Non-ITaP staff members are restricted to Level I Authorization.

  2. A “Data Center Access Authorization” request must be on file for each individual who is authorized to enter the Data Center. Enter a ticket via support.purdue.edu (New Issue – Quick Templates – SO.DatCenAccess)

  3. Visitors to the Data Center are to adhere to the visitors’ guidelines (see section 3.2).

  4. A data center management employee must accompany visitors in the Data Center, or another authorized employee, at all times while in the Data Center. Exceptions to this policy must have approval of the Data Center Manager or Data Center Coordinator (Jon Miller/Todd Turner respectively).

  5. All persons, with the exception of Infrastructure employees, must sign in when entering the Data Center to document the time and purpose of their visit. They must also sign out when leaving.

  6. For the Freehafer Hall Data Center all visitors and authorized staff must enter through the south entrance.

 

Note: The term “visitor” is defined as anyone who:

 

  1. does not work in the Data Center;

  2. is not an Infrastructure staff member;

  3. does not have Level I authorization to the Data Center;

  4. does not have Level II authorization to the Data Center.

 

2.2 Equipment in an ITaP Data Center

 

In an effort to maximize security and minimize disruptions, the following policies apply to all equipment housed in an ITaP Data Center.

 

  1. An electronic request must be completed for all equipment installations, removals, and renames via support.purdue.edu.

  2. Operations staff will deny entry to authorized staff who intends to install, remove, or rename equipment without an installation form on file.

 

2.3 Hardware/Software Maintenance & Upgrades of Production Equipment

 

  1. Authorized employees may perform maintenance/repair on an as-needed basis 24 hours/7 days a week.

 

 

3.0 Procedures

 

3.1 Access Authorization

 

All employees must have proper authorization to gain access to an ITaP Data Center. Based upon the frequency of access and the home department of the person requesting access, there are two levels of authorization. The procedures to acquire authorization, at each level, are detailed below:

 

3.1.1 Level I Authorization

 

  1. The employee requesting access to a Data Center must complete an electronic request using the SO.DatCenAccess Quick Templates at support.purdue.edu.

  2. His/her director/manager will authorize the request submitted via item 1.

  3. After director/manager approval, the Hardware Services & Operations (HSO) Director will approve via the tech notes in the electronic request

  4. After approval by the HSO Director approves the request, the IT Infrastructure Operations Security Coordinator will then process the request.

  5. The employee will be added to the authorization database.

  6. The Security Coordinator will provide quarterly audits on who has access to the data centers.

  7. The employee will be authorized to enter the Data Center, but will NOT have card swipe access. The Operations staff on duty will verify employee authorization before allowing the employee to enter the Data Center.

  8. The employee must log in/out when entering/exiting the Data Center. The purpose of the visit must be documented.

  9. Level I Authorization is the standard access policy for non-ITaP staff members.

 

3.1.2 Level II Authorization

 

  1. The employee requesting access to a Data Center must complete an electronic request using the SO.DatCenAccess Quick Templates at support.purdue.edu.

  2. His/her director/manager will authorize the request submitted via item 1.

  3. After director/manager approval, the Hardware Services & Operations (HSO) Director will approve via the tech notes in the electronic request

  4. After approval by the HSO Director approves the request, the IT Infrastructure Operations Security Coordinator will then process the request.

  5. The employee will be added to the authorization database.

  6. The Security Coordinator will provide quarterly audits on who has access to the data centers.

  7. The employee will be authorized to enter the Data Center and will be given card swipe access.

  8. The employee must log in/out when entering/exiting the Data Center. The purpose of the visit must be documented.

 

3.2 Visitor Guidelines

 

Anyone who does not does not report to the Data Center on a daily basis, is not an Infrastructure employee, or who does not have Level I/Level II authorization is considered a visitor. All visitors to an ITaP Data Center must adhere to the following guidelines:

 

  1. Visitors must log in/out when entering/exiting the Data Center. The purpose of the visit must be documented.

  2. A data center management employee or another authorized employee must accompany visitors at all times while in the Data Center. All exceptions must have the approval of the Data Center Manager or Coordinator (Jon Miller/Todd Turner respectively).

  3. Visits to an ITaP Data Center should be coordinated through the Data Center Coordinator at least 24 hours in advance.

 

3.3 Audit Procedures

 

  1. The IT Infrastructure Security Coordinator will send a list of authorized employees to each director on a quarterly basis (January, April, July, and October) for his/her review and verification.

  2. Each director will review and update the list of authorized employees and return it to the Security Coordinator within two weeks.

  3. Each Semester, all student employees will be removed from the access data base and must renew access authorization if employment continues.

  4. Each (non-data center management) employee must renew access authorization annually during the announced renewal period.

 

3.4 Equipment Installation

 

The employee performing the installation will follow the procedures outlined under the ITaP Change Management Program (http://www.itap.purdue.edu/infrastructure/operations/change/).

 

3.5 Equipment Removal

 

The employee performing the removal will follow procedures outlined under the ITaP Change Management Program (http://www.itap.purdue.edu/infrastructure/operations/change/).

 

3.6 Equipment Renaming

 

The employee performing the rename will follow procedures outlined under the ITaP Change Management Program (http://www.itap.purdue.edu/infrastructure/operations/change/).

title: Audit Control
content:
Goals

Implement hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in information systems that contain or use electronic protected health information.

Review

This policy and related procedures shall be reviewed at least every 3 years.

Mixed Responsibility

For HIPAA-covered systems, the Sherlock environment provides logging and auditing capabilities and policies that supplement, and in some cases, replace, the normal SDSC HUBzero policies.  In those cases, SDSC HUBzero is responsible for auditing related to the operation of HUBzero web application science gateway itself;  SDSC Sherlock is responsible for all other auditing, e.g., operating system-level events, anti-virus software activity, etc...

Auditable Events (AU-2)

HUBzero deployments must be capable of auditing the following events, defined by control AU-2, and must have procedures to do so:

  • Server alerts and error messages
  • User log-on and log-off (successful or unsuccessful;
  • System administration activities;
  • Modification of privileges and access
  • Start up and shut down
  • Modifications to the application
  • Application alerts and error messages
  • Configuration changes
  • Account creation, modification, or deletion

The system has the capability to log events as provided by all Linux OS distributions and included software packages.  In addition, the HUBzero software can log authentication events, as well as access requests and the HTTP result code for the requests.  General usage inside the HUBzero software is logged in the database table "jos_activity_logs".  This is supplemented with additional logging implemented by "components".  Each software component is responsible for defining more specific auditable events and logging their use in additional database tables.

Which events are relevant is a function of HUBzero’s primary goals, which are to restore integrity and availability and protect confidentiality. Providing forensic evidence for law enforcement's use isn’t a concern although it may happen incidentally. As a defense against compromise, all authentication attempts (successes and failures) across all mechanisms supported by the Apache web service should be logged, including use of cookies, WebDAV, or SVN over HTTP. Repeated failures should result in bans to protect against brute force attacks, except where implemented separately for federated identity providers.  Bans are auditable events, to address availability complaints and ensure the proper function of the mechanism.

For availability purposes, mail (SMTP) events should be logged. The IP addresses of servers attempting to deliver spam should also be logged to block repeated attempts to abuse the mail system.

Similarly, SSH activity should be logged and processed to automatically block repeated attacks, as well as flag that activity. 

Content of Audit Records (AU-3)

HUBzero deployments must generate audit records containing information that establishes what type of event occurred, when the event occurred, where the event occurred, the source of the event, the outcome of the event, and the identity of any individuals or subjects associated with the event (see control AU-3).  All authentication attempts (successes and failures) across all mechanisms supported by the Apache web service are logged, including use of cookies, WebDAV, SVN over HTTP. Repeated failures result in bans to protect against brute force attacks, except for Google and Shibboleth because these authentication mechanisms have their own protection mechanisms. Bans are logged with the time and IP address, and in the case of an account suspension, which user account was implicated.

HUBzero software logs usernames, IP addresses, URLs accessed, time, protocol used (e.g., version of TLS), and the nature of the events (e.g., password changes, failed access, Google authentication, Shibboleth records, and bans).  The default logging format of other services is used.

HUBzero also logs mail (SMTP) events. The IP addresses of servers attempting to deliver spam are also logged to block repeated attempts to abuse the mail system. HUBzero also logs all requests made to the web server, which are processed with regular expressions to detect unusual activity and automatically block some forms of attacks (e.g., SQL injection). Similarly, SSH activity is logged and processed with regular expressions to automatically block repeated attacks, as well as flag that activity in automated emails sent to administrators.

Audit Storage Capacity (AU-4)

HUBzero relies on the virtual environments where it is deployed to provide disk space as needed (e.g., SDSC Sherlock, SDSC RDS and AWS).

historical, for reference only: 

HUBzero uses LVM to flexibly manage storage space, in combination with monitoring of storage status every 5 minutes and alarms with the Xymon system. The Xymon system monitors the disk space available for logs, and sends alerts when reaching 90 (yellow) and 95 (red) percent capacity. Storage organization follows CIS benchmark suggestions to separate audit storage from data storage, making the whole more robust against failures, abuses, and unexpected usage levels. A pool of spare storage that can be assigned as needed is available. Audit storage has a capacity that exceeds previously encountered peak levels by at least 10%.

Response to Audit Processing Failures (AU-5)

When running out of storage space, the logging mechanisms used by HUBzero deployments, including needed services as well as the HUBzero software, must discard the oldest event logs so new activity can still be logged (see control AU-5).

Time Stamps (AU-8)

HUBzero records timestamp information at a granularity of 1 second. Time is synchronized using a stratum 1 server. Synchronization status is monitored by the Xymon system.

Retention (AU-11)

As a baseline, standard Linux OS and service logs (e.g., Apache) must be collected for 30 days and retained for up to 1 year through the use of monthly backup images.  Database tables used for logging must also collect data for 30 days, relying on monthly backup images to provide log access for up to a year.  If a hub is retired (no longer in production service), only one recent backup will be kept for up to a year.

AU-12 Audit Generation

HUBzero deployments must:

a. Provide audit record generation capability for the auditable events defined in AU-2 for components and services managed by HUBzero;

b. Allow System Administrators and CMS administrators, as applicable, to select which auditable events are to be audited by specific components of the information system; and

c. Generate audit records for the events defined in AU-2 d. with the content defined in AU-3.

Hardware Mechanisms

A central logging stand-alone host is used to receive logs and process them.  In addition to local copies are kept on the servers, and more copies kept on backup servers.  All copies contribute to log retention.

Software and Procedural Mechanisms (excluding Sherlock environment):

On UNIX servers, system activity is logged in various files in the directory /var/log, which are examined by the fail2ban mechanism. Excessive failures result in a ban of the IP address concerned, with a different sensitivity depending on whether the address belongs to the HUBzero network or if it is external. This applies to both web site logins (including WebDAV) and SSH logins (including sftp). Suspicious network activity also results in a ban of the IP addresses involved.

Historical, for reference only (not in place at SDSC): 

Information gathered from system logs shall be automatically and periodically filtered by blacklisting known routine events representing normal activity, and sending for review all other events to system administrators.  In addition, a monitoring system shall be used to log resource usage and relevant indicators of system activity.

All events received by a system's logging mechanism (whether rsyslog, system-journald or other) shall be filtered as described above.  On HIPAA-covered hubs, a system administrator shall also review Apache access and error logs using a similar filter.

The syslog records are sent to a centralized logging system. There, activity deemed normal is automatically filtered out using logcheck software, and everything else is emailed to system administrators on an hourly basis. Administrators on duty are expected to read these emails, looking for signs of trouble.

Reviews shall be done every hour if possible, and at least once every regular business day. It is sufficient that a single system administrator does this, but it is OK to have more. System administrators are responsible for coordinating this.

All system administrators must receive these emails, which contains log events triaged and filtered through the logcheck software. Only email accounts hosted on Purdue systems or a provider nationally recognized for secure email (e.g., Gmail) shall be used for subscribing to the list.

The Apache logs are filtered locally through logcheck software, and reports of unexpected activity are emailed hourly to administrators. 

CMS administrators are responsible for monitoring the PHP error log files. The PHP error logs are automatically monitored by size, and sudden increases result in alerts sent to CMS administrators.  CMS administrators are responsible for reacting to these emails and handling the related issues.

A designated HUBzero system administrator must be reachable via telephone and answer calls from Purdue IOC outside business hours.  After such a call, system administrators must:
        make a best effort attempt at resolving the situation
        Report findings that may affect customer experiences, or that may be of interest, to the entire HUBzero team using a Slack channel.
        Given Slack messages, gateway managers will contact Hub owners and appropriate external staff as required.

title: External Authenticators
content:
Single sign-on (SSO) is a element of access control of multiple related, yet independent, software systems. A user logs in with a single ID and password to gain access to a system without using different usernames or passwords, or in some configurations seamlessly sign on at each system.

Benefits of using single sign-on include:

    Mitigate risk for access to 3rd-party sites (user passwords not stored or managed externally)
    Reduce password fatigue from different user name and password combinations
    Reduce time spent re-entering passwords for the same identity
    Reduce IT costs due to lower number of IT help desk calls about passwords

SSO shares centralized authentication servers that all other applications and systems use for authentication purposes and combines this with techniques to ensure that users do not have to actively enter their credentials more than once.

 

CILOGON

A hub administrator must register at http://cilogon.org/oauth2/register

Enter a Client Name.
Enter a Contact Email Address.
Enter a home URL (the URL of your hub - hubzero.org, for example).
Callback URLS should be:

**<hostname> should be replaced with the HUB URL.  If you have more than one hub instance, include a redirect URL set for each host that you will wish to use CiLogon.
   
https://<hostname>/index.php?option=com_users&task=user.link&authenticator=cilogon
https://<hostname>/index.php?option=com_users&task=user.login&authenticator=cilogon
https://<hostname>/administrator/index.php?option=com_login&task=login&authenticator=cilogon

Select all SCOPES (email, edu.., openid, profile, org.cilogon...).
Leave blank - Refresh Token Lifetime.
Leave blank - Issuer.

CiLogon will process the registration and if approved a client id and client secret will be provided and must be added to the "Authenticator - CILogon" plugin in the Adminstrator Interface (/administrator) to enable to plugin.  Once enabled, users may log into your hub via credentials provided by CiLogon.

title: Installation
content:
Target Audience

This document and the installation and maintenance of a HUBzero system has a target audience of experienced Linux administrators.

Minimum System Requirements

A typical starter HUBzero installation might consist of a single physical server with dual 64-bit quad-core CPUs, 24 Gigabytes of RAM and a terabyte of disk.

Production systems should try to not limit hardware resources, HUBzero is designed to run on systems with many CPU cores and lots of RAM. If you are looking for a system to run a small site with limited physical or virtual resources this is probably not the system for you. However, for demonstration or development purposes we often create VM images with less than a gigabyte of RAM and 5 gigabytes of disk. While fully functional, these virtual machines would only be suitable for a single user doing development or testing.

System Architecture

All hardware, filesystem partitions, RAID configurations, backup models, security models, etc. and base configurations of the hosts (SSH server, network, etc.) are the responsibility of the system administrator managing the host.

The HUBzero software expects to be installed on a headless server from a minimal ISO with only one network interface (required by OpenVZ) with an MTU no less than '1500'.  System accounts must not be created with an id of 1000 or greater - more about that in a forthcoming section.

 

 

End of Life for Debian Linux Distribution 

HUBzero support for the Debian Linux distribution is no longer available, effective August 27, 2020. 

You may continue to use Debian for a hub installation, however, support for HUBzero operating system packages and other related software will no longer receive updates.  Maintenance and support for installed software, including security updates are the responsibility of the individual hub system administrators. 

HUBzero will continue to offer its suite of open-source software on the CentOS Linux distribution, allowing us to focus our efforts on maintaining and improving our code-base, as well as bringing you additional features and upgrades such as Docker which replaces OpenVZ for hub tool session containers.
 
For support or help migrating a hub to CentOS, please contact info@hubzero.org.

title: a 1 ii (D) Information System Activity Review
content:
Goal

"Implement procedures to regularly review records of information system activity, such as audit logs, access reports, and security incident tracking reports."

Policy

The goal of this policy is to allow timely detection of problems and anomalies so that corrective actions can be taken before they create or become incidents, or to initiate incident response as appropriate.

HUBzero will develop and maintain procedures to review records of information system activity on a periodic basis.  This responsibility may be delegated to staff operating the environments where VMs are provisioned for HUBzero and in which they operate.  Additional reviews will be done as needed where incidents are reported or suspected, as defined in our Incident Response Plan. These procedures will use automated mechanisms to monitor logs and service statuses and extract relevant information, to generate alerts as appropriate.  Alerts will be directed to active duty and designated on-call personnel, of which there will always be at least one individual.  These individuals must keep their contact information up-to-date in the appropriate lists and system configurations, and maintain any required services.

System Activity Review Procedures

RDS Environment (not HIPAA-covered, not FISMA-certified):

Most of the system activity review is done by RDS staff, using their procedures and plans.  HUBzero also created a number of regularly run checks via the "cron" system, sending emails alerts to "sysadmins@hubzero.org".  In addition, the "PRTG" monitoring system will send emails to that list.  Every day, hubzero system administrators will:

  • Review emails sent to "sysadmins@hubzero.org" and take appropriate action, when necessary escalating issues to RDS staff by creating tickets by sending an email to "support@sdsc.edu" or communicating via "Slack".
  • Check the "PRTG Desktop" application status for our VMs, or review emails sent individually to system administrators with the subject "[SDSC Unified Monitor]"
  • Inform HUBzero management of any downtime incurred via the Slack channel "trouble" in the hubzero Slack workspace.

Sherlock Environment (HIPAA-covered):

Most of the system activity review is done by Sherlock staff, using their procedures and plans. Automated alerts that are in the scope of HUBzero responsibilities will be emailed to "sysadmins@hubzero.org".  HUBzero also created a number of regularly run checks via the "cron" system, sending emails alerts to "sysadmins@hubzero.org".  Every day, hubzero system administrators will:

  • Review emails sent to "sysadmins@hubzero.org" and take appropriate action, if necessary creating tickets by sending an email to "sherlocksupport@sdsc.edu" to request assistance from the Sherlock team.
  • Inform HUBzero management of any downtime incurred via the Slack channel "trouble" in the hubzero Slack workspace.
  • Managers pass this information along to designated contacts for each site operated by hubzero for anything of significant duration and importance.

Events to be reviewed at least weekly are defined by control AU-2:

  • Unsuccessful log-on attempts that result in a locked account/node (see table "jos_users_log_auth", status='blocked');
  • Configuration changes;
  • Application alerts and error messages;
  • System administration activities;
  • Modification of privileges and access; and
  • Account creation, modification, or deletion.

Purdue Environment (historical):

Every day:

  • Review system changes reported by rkhunter
  • Check if there are updates to apply to Debian systems
    • Login on control.hubzero.org
    • Run /root/bin/patch_pkgs to patch non-production systems and restart affected services
    • Run /root/bin/patch_production to patch production systems and restart affected services
  • Check if Xymon reported anything of importance.
  • Check if there were any backup errors
  • Read the "logcheck" automated emails, looking for anything warranting correction or response.
  • Check whether the installation of new kernel versions might have caused Yellow or Red alert for disk space on /boot. Remove extra, unneeded kernels that can consume all the space on /boot. See OS-specific procedures for suggested and example commands.

 

Related to:

NIST SP 800-53 control families "SI System and information integrity" and "AU Audit and Accountability":
(AU-1) Audit and Accountability Policy and Procedures
(AU-2) Auditable Events
(AU-3) Content of Audit Records
(AU-4) Audit Storage Capacity
(AU-5) Response to Audit Processing Failures
(AU-6) Audit Review, Analysis, and Reporting

 

Old wiki versions of this policy are at: https://help.hubzero.org/groups/hubzero_hipaa/wiki/164308a1iiDInformationSystemActivityReview

title: FISMA Security Control Traceability Matrix
content:
A Security Control Traceability Matrix (SCTM) is part of a particular System's Security Plan (SSP).  Controls are sets of policies and procedures defined and followed to achieve a security goal.  The SCTM has 3 types of "controls":

  • Common: "A security control that is inheritable by one or more organizational information systems."  That means we can define these controls once for all, or a group of, systems operated by HUBzero in the Sherlock environment.
  • System: "A security control for an information system that has not been designated as a common security control or the portion of a hybrid control that is to be implemented within an information system."  That means the control is specific for a particular system's requirements and is not applicable to others.  For example, ncihub has hub-specific policies described at https://ncihub.org/projects/policies/notes.
  • Hybrid: "A security control that is implemented in an information system in part as a common control and in part as a system control."

At the time of this writing, HUBzero only operates one FISMA-certified system, ncihub.org, so all controls for this FISMA-Low system will be described here.  If more FISMA-certified systems were to be operated, this document should define "common" controls that would apply to all systems hosted by HUBzero in the Sherlock environment, and separate documents should define the "system" controls for each. 

This SCTM provides a mapping of controls to existing HUBzero policies defined elsewhere, and as needed defines additional policies and procedures for the implementation of a control.    Should this document conflict with a particular System's Security Plan and this document contains more recent versions of controls, the SSP shall be examined for any needed updates, and the updated SSP shall be followed.

This document was prepared using the NCI System Security Plan template that used NIST Special Publication 800-53 revision 4, which is valid but to be withdrawn on September 23, 2021.  At time of this writing (January 2021), the NIST Special Publication 800-53 revision 5, "Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations" is the most recent version, but we do not use it yet.  Please refer to revision 4 for the definitions of controls and control enhancements.  The NVD has a particularly useful organization of the controls, by family and by impact baseline.

Important: The text used in the NCI System Security Plan template does not match exactly the SP 800-53 control descriptions because "assignments" have been made.  These assignments represent decisions made by NCI, and the text in the SSP template takes precedence over the more generic SP 800-53.

title: Restoring Borg Backups
content:
Borg Backups uses a repository for each host, and an archive (that means a successful backup) for each partition and date.  Restores can be done in these manners:

  • Initiated from the client, restoring specific directories, files, or an entire partition
  • Restoring an entire host is done by restoring each filesystem one at a time (filesystems are backed up one by one)
  • Specific archives can be mounted on the server, archive4
  • Specific archives can be mounted on the client

Exception: PURR Data Depot Backups

The descriptions below do not directly apply to PURR's Data Depot storage.  Those backups are done directly on archive4, by user "borg-data.rcac.purdue.edu", from an SSHFS mount of Data Depot.  Equivalents to the scripts described below are in that user's home directory. Otherwise the same instructions apply.

List Backup Archives

Use the script /usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_client_list to make your life easier.  It will print a list of all images for each partition, followed by repository information, and an explanation of the names of the backups.  Note that the argument is the hostname of the backup server, not the client.  For example:

# /usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_client_list archive4.hubzero.org

Available backup archives:
-2018-02-28.19-30-03                 Wed, 2018-02-28 19:30:05 [83befb49232bf3002609668d3299f63dbc775d92abcf718aa29c1bd94050b37b]
-2018-03-31.19-30-04                 Sat, 2018-03-31 19:30:08 [a89a0160968a39e6cfab096b7b66676b3743c5dc374248908b567da99dc9465c]
-2018-04-15.19-30-03                 Sun, 2018-04-15 19:30:05 [4ea04a38b32c4dca4d4b90664c84ddb74bb6b382427eeb6e8875992250c67d08]
-2018-04-22.19-30-04                 Sun, 2018-04-22 19:30:05 [a61c53bcfa54e621b2206e47f24b5b6fbdde9faf2f4754ee6380de522e3292e6]
-2018-04-29.19-30-07                 Sun, 2018-04-29 19:30:15 [4f7c71ae58f083ad54e3ce3a7d44b4c5949839308b6787f7ea2ac4ec57f83c90]

...

Partitions are backed up as follows:
/ backed up as -date

Restore Files with /usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_client_restore

On the client, figure out which archive you want to use (see above).  Important:  cd into the directory where you want the restored files to go.  If you don't want to overwrite things, create a new directory for the restore, and cd into it.  Then run the script, for example:

/usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_client_restore archive4.hubzero.org db-2018-09-13.03-06-28 re:db/dev/deeds/submit/sessions/.*/[0-9]*/output/submit.finish

where the last argument is a pattern recognized by Borg.  A prefix tells Borg which kind of pattern it is, e.g., "sh:", "re:" or "pp:".  If you don't use a prefix, you may be surprised by the files you do or don't get.  You don't need a prefix if you just specify the path to a directory.

You may wish to edit the script first, and add options like "--list" or "--dry-run" to the borg extract command.

WARNING: if you restore specific files only, directories above those files may be restored with root:root ownerships and default permissions instead of the original ones.

Restore Files with Borg Extract

The steps are:

  • Setup the environment for the commands
    • Borg environment variables are useful
    • "LANG=en_US.UTF-8" may be needed
  • Run "borg list" to figure out the name of the archive you want to restore from.  Note that the time and date are when the backup STARTED, not when it finished, whereas rsync backup snapshots have the time when it finished
  • Change directories to where you want files restored
    • Note that the whole directory hierarchy is recreated, e.g., restoring /var/log/audit in place results in /var/log/audit/var/log/audit.  A "mv" or "cp" operation is then needed to complete the restore.
    • Extraneous files are not removed
  • Run "borg extract --numeric-owner /path/to/repo::filesystem-date /path/to/directory" to restore a directory from the backup done on a certain date

Example 1, restore a single file:

# setup environment so the commands use SSH with the correct private key
borg_server=archive4.hubzero.org
hostname=`hostname -f`
BORG_RSH="ssh -i /usr/share/adm/ogre/secret/hosts/$hostname/borg_$hostname"
export BORG_RSH
BORG_REPO=ssh://borg-$hostname@$borg_server/repo
export BORG_REPO

# figure out which archive you want 
borg list borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo

# This fails because the path must not include the mount point:

devsubmit-64:~# borg extract --numeric-owner borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::-2018-05-05.00-11-06 /opt/submit/SubmitCommand.py
Include pattern '/opt/submit/SubmitCommand.py' never matched.

# This works because "/" (the mount point) was removed from the path to the wanted file:

devsubmit-64:~# borg extract --numeric-owner borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::-2018-05-05.00-11-06 opt/submit/SubmitCommand.py
devsubmit-64:~# ll /root/opt/submit/
total 72K
drwx------ 2 root    root 4.0K May 19 06:47 .
drwx------ 3 root    root 4.0K May 19 06:47 ..
-rw-r----- 1 clarksm apps  60K Apr 30 11:52 SubmitCommand.py
devsubmit-64:~#

Example 2 (more automation, appropriate for restoring an OpenVZ container from within):

# setup environment so the commands use SSH with the correct private key
borg_server=archive4.hubzero.org
hostname=`hostname -f`
BORG_RSH="ssh -i /usr/share/adm/ogre/secret/hosts/$hostname/borg_$hostname"
export BORG_RSH
BORG_REPO=ssh://borg-$hostname@$borg_server/repo
export BORG_REPO

partition=/
# cd $partition 
date=2018-02-28
LANG=en_US.UTF-8
sp=`echo ${partition#/} | tr '/' '_'`
archive_name=`borg list borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo | grep -- ^$sp-$date | cut -f1 -d ' '`
echo restoring $archive_name
time borg extract borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::$archive_name


Example 3: restore all partitions, e.g., on an OpenVZ host

date=2018-02-28
plist=`grep -e xfs -e ext[2-4] /etc/fstab | grep -v -e '^#' -e /mnt/db-raid |  awk '{ print $2 }'`
for partition in $plist; do
  case $partition in

  "/var/lib/vz")
    # OpenVZ: backup only templates
    # backup running containers from the inside
    partition="/var/lib/vz/template"
    ;;
    
  "/vz")
    partition="/vz/template"
    ;;

  # don't backup KVM raw files, backup the image from the inside of the VM
  "/var/lib/libvirt/images")
    continue
    ;;

  # don't backup raw database partitions, instead backup the logical dumps
  "/var/lib/mysql"*)
    continue
    ;;

  "/export/mysql")
    continue
    ;;

  "/var/lib/postgresql")
    continue
    ;;

  # don't backup temporary MySQL table scratch space
  "/var/mysqltmp")
    continue
    ;;

  "/tmp")
    continue
    ;;

  # Don't backup Pegasus scratch space
  "/pegtmp")
    continue
    ;;

  # don't backup the Debian repo mirrors
  "/var/spool/apt-mirror")
    continue
    ;;
  esac
  sp=`echo ${partition#/} | tr '/' '_'`
  archive_name=`borg list borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo | grep -- ^$sp-$date | cut -f1 -d ' '`
  echo restoring $archive_name
  cd $partition 
  time borg extract borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::$archive_name
  echo you still need to move or copy the restored files at $partition/$partition
done

Example 4: Floating IPs (NanoHUB home, apps)

Floating IPs are backed up by the script /usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_run_floating

 

# setup environment so the commands use SSH with the correct private key
hostname=`cat /etc/borg/float.repo`
borg_server=archive4.hubzero.org
usernamelong=borg-$hostname
username=${usernamelong:0:32}
# BatchMode sets ServerAliveInterval to 300 and ServerAliveCountMax to 3, so use "borg --lock-wait 1000"
BORG_RSH="ssh -i /usr/share/adm/ogre/secret/hosts/$hostname/borg_$hostname -o BatchMode=yes"
export BORG_RSH
BORG_REPO=ssh://$username@$borg_server/repo
export BORG_REPO

TEMP=/root/tmp
export TEMP
mkdir -p /root/tmp

# figure out which partition you want to restore
cat /etc/borg/floats
partition=/export/home
sp=`echo ${partition#/} | tr '/' '_'`

# figure out which archive you want
borg list $username@$borg_server:repo

cd /root/tmp
borg extract --numeric-owner $username@$borg_server:repo::export_home-2018-05-21.20-12-05 export/home/nanohub/mmh/notebooks
mv export/home/nanohub/mmh/notebooks /export/home/nanohub/mmh/notebooks

 

  

Borg Mount

For OpenVZ containers look below.

"borg mount" can be very useful to verify a backup, by doing something like "diff -qr" or "rsync --dry-run".  Similarly to the above:

  • Check that "fuse" can be used -- this may not work inside some OpenVZ containers
  • Setup the environment for the commands
  • Run "borg list" to figure out the name of the archive you want to restore from
  • Change directories to where you want files restored
  • Run "borg mount"

Example:

LANG=en_US.UTF-8
mkdir /mnt/borg
borg mount -o ro borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::(archive name) /mnt/borg

Example 2: Mount archives for all partitions under /mnt/borg-(partition)

Select the date below and the archives from that date will be used:

date=2018-02-28 

for m in `ls -d /mnt/borg*`; do
  echo $m
  umount $m
done 

rmdir /mnt/*

# setup environment so the commands use SSH with the correct private key
borg_server=archive4.hubzero.org
hostname=`hostname -f`
BORG_RSH="ssh -i /usr/share/adm/ogre/secret/hosts/$hostname/borg_$hostname"
export BORG_RSH
BORG_REPO=ssh://borg-$hostname@$borg_server/repo
export BORG_REPO

plist=`grep -e xfs -e ext[2-4] /etc/fstab | grep -v -e '^#' -e /mnt/db-raid |  awk '{ print $2 }'`
for partition in $plist; do
  case $partition in

  "/var/lib/vz")
    # OpenVZ: backup only templates
    # backup running containers from the inside
    partition="/var/lib/vz/template"
    ;;
    
  "/vz")
    partition="/vz/template"
    ;;

  # don't backup KVM raw files, backup the image from the inside of the VM
  "/var/lib/libvirt/images")
    continue
    ;;

  # don't backup raw database partitions, instead backup the logical dumps
  "/var/lib/mysql"*)
    continue
    ;;

  "/export/mysql")
    continue
    ;;

  "/var/lib/postgresql")
    continue
    ;;

  # don't backup temporary MySQL table scratch space
  "/var/mysqltmp")
    continue
    ;;

  "/tmp")
    continue
    ;;

  # Don't backup Pegasus scratch space
  "/pegtmp")
    continue
    ;;

  # don't backup the Debian repo mirrors
  "/var/spool/apt-mirror")
    continue
    ;;
  esac

  sp=`echo ${partition#/} | tr '/' '_'`
  mkdir -p /mnt/borg-$sp
  # archive_name=$sp-$date
  archive_name=`borg list borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo | grep -- ^$sp-$date | cut -f1 -d ' '`
  echo borg mount -o ro borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::$archive_name /mnt/borg-$sp
done

# Use the mount points to do an rsync (10x slower than borg extract) or whatever else you need

for m in `ls -d /mnt/borg*`; do
  echo $m
  p=`echo /${m#/mnt/borg-} |  tr '_' '/'`
  time rsync -vcax --dry-run $p/ $m$p/ | grep -v -e puppet -e ^tmp -e /tars/ -e ^run -e root/.cache/borg/ -e ^var/lib/apt/ -e var/cache/ -e var/backups/ -e var/log/letsencrypt/ -e sftp/ -e var/lib/dpkg -e var/lib/spamassassin/
  echo
done

Example 3: Borg Mount and OpenVZ containers: not recommended

Unless the container has access to fuse, the mount will have to be done on the underlying OpenVZ host. This complicates things.

# somehow when run in a terminal as root, it's different than from this script?
export BORG_UNKNOWN_UNENCRYPTED_REPO_ACCESS_IS_OK=yes
# on archive4, invoking borg locally sets this off when it's run from cron later
export BORG_RELOCATED_REPO_ACCESS_IS_OK=yes

# Does archive4 allow connections from the OpenVZ server?
vzlist
hostname=labs.catalyzecare.org
ctid=2010
ll /vz/private/$ctid/usr/share/adm/ogre/secret/hosts/$hostname/borg_$hostname

# Allow access to the repository on archive4 from the OpenVZ host (normally access is only from the container):
hostname=labs.catalyzecare.org
cat /home/borg/borg-$hostname/.ssh/authorized_keys
vi .ssh/authorized_keys

# Back on the OpenVZ server:
BORG_RSH="ssh -i /vz/private/$ctid/usr/share/adm/ogre/secret/hosts/$hostname/borg_$hostname"

borg list borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo
archive_name=
LANG=en_US.UTF-8
borg mount -o ro borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::$archive_name /mnt/borg

# verify without checksums (very fast)
rsync -vcax --dry-run /vz/private/$ctid/ /mnt/borg/ | grep -v -e ^tmp -e ^run -e root/.cache/borg/ -e ^var/lib/apt/ -e var/cache/ -e var/backups/ -e var/log/letsencrypt/ 

# verify with checksums (-c option): slow but thorough, this is effectively a complete restore operation
rsync -vcax --dry-run /vz/private/$ctid/ /mnt/borg/ | grep -v -e ^tmp -e ^run -e root/.cache/borg/ -e ^var/lib/apt/ -e var/cache/ -e var/backups/ -e var/log/letsencrypt/

title: Account Management
content:
If a hub doesn't have a explicit policy on account management such as login failures, the defaults will be as follows.  Note that NCIPhub has explicitly set such policies (see the hub-specific information for NCIPhub).  Account management policies can be applied by following the account management procedures.

SSH Key Management Policies

See this sub-page

Password Reset Frequency

Password resets will be rate limited to 2/hour per user.

Login Failures and Bans

By default, password login attempts will be rate limited to 10 in 2 hours, per user, with a ban of up to 2 hours.  The mechanism used by the CMS counts the number of failures over the number of hours specified and blocks logins until the oldest failure falls outside that window.  So if the oldest failure was nearly two hours ago, then it could be possible for someone to be banned only for a few minutes.  Although 50 in 5 hours and 10 in 1 hour is the same rate, the implementation is such that the former can result in a ban of 5 hours and the latter, a ban of 1 hour maximum. 

If an IP address is abused to attack many accounts, that address will get banned by engaging the "fail2ban" mechanism, which must be turned on.  If 5 accounts/hour get banned from the same IP address, then that IP address will be blocked by calling fail2ban. 

The procedure for the implementation of this policy is in the administrative section, "Account Management"

Login Failures and Bans -- Desired Future Policy

By default, password login attempts for (IP address, user) pairs will be rate limited to 10/hour.  If an IP address is abused to attack many accounts, many (IP address, user) pairs will get banned by engaging the "fail2ban" mechanism, which must be turned on.  If 10 pairs/hour get banned then the IP address will be blocked by calling fail2ban.  If a user account gets attacked from many different IP addresses, the account must get locked to protect against distributed attacks.

Password Strength

NIH FISMA Requirements

  • Password length must be at least eight (8) characters in length.
  • Passwords are required to be a combination of at least one (1) character from each of the four (4) character categories:
    • Capital letters (A‐Z),
    • Lower case letters (a‐z),
    • Numeric characters (0‐9), and
    • Special characters (e.g., !@#$%^&*()_+|~‐=\`{}[]:";'<>?,./).
    • Maximum Password Age/Change frequency: Must be changed at least every one hundred twenty (120) days.
  • New password must be different from the previous six (6) generations of passwords.  This can be satisfied by requiring passwords to be different from the passwords used in the preceeding 6*120 = 720 days.

General HIPAA Requirements

Hubs needing regulatory compliance or having other security concerns, the following additional characteristics must be mandated:

    Must contain more than 4 unique characters
    Must not contain your name or parts of your name
    Must not contain your username
    Must be different than the previous password (re-use of the same password will not be allowed for one (1) year)
    Passwords must be changed every N days, where N is a year or less.

Regular Requirements

For hubs without special security requirements, passwords must at a minimum have the following characteristics (CMS administrative interface path Users -> Members -> Passwords):

    Must contain at least 1 letter
    Must contain at least 1 number or punctuation mark
    Must be at least 8 characters long
    Passwords must be changed every N days, where N is 5 years or less.

Password Hashes

The password hashing mechanism must use SHA512.

title: Account Management
content:
See also "Review of Account Privileges" and under Technical Procedures, "Termination Procedures".

System Use Notifications

At login a banner should be displayed on some hubs to state things like "usage may be monitored, recorded, and subject to audit; etc, etc, etc".  The procedure to change this banner is:

  • Login to the administrative interface, a.k.a. backend, at /administrator
  • Navigate to "Menu Manager: Menus"
  • Under "Title", click on "Default"
  • In the list of menu items, under "Title", click on "Login"
  • Enter the banner in the field "Login Description Text"

Password Reset Frequency Limits

The procedure to configure password reset limits is:

  • Consult policy to figure out the number of allowed password resets/hour for the hub in question. 
  • Login to the administrative interface, a.k.a. backend, at /administrator
  • Navigate to Users -> Members -> Options icon (wrench and hammer)
  • In the popup window, go to the tab “Login Settings”
  • Change the “Maximum Reset Count” per time period "Time in Hours" to match

 

Login Failures and Bans

The policy corresponding to this procedure is "Account Management"

The mechanism bans users (i.e., by temporary lockout) that fail more than X logins over an interval of Y hours.  If many users get banned from the same IP address, then that address gets banned by calling fail2ban. 

The duration of individual user bans is up to Y hours, depending on when failed logins "expire" by being outside the time window being considered (the last Y hours).  The duration of the IP bans is set in fail2ban.  There are UI pictures in the regular documentation:

Home › Documentation › 2.1.0 › Internal Docs › Fail2Ban - CMS

which is at fail2ban__cms

This procedure complements that documentation:

  • Consult policy to figure out how banning should be escalated depending on the failure rates
  • Login to the administrative interface, a.k.a. backend, at /administrator
  • Navigate to Users -> Members -> Options icon (wrench and hammer)
  • In the popup window, go to the tab “Login Settings”
  • "Maximum Failed Login Attempts" refers to the number of login failures for an individual account.  The "Time in Hours" determines the rate and the maximum duration of a ban.
  • Select a log retention period to limit the size of the storage, and prevent slower logins when it gets too large.
  • "Fail2ban" refers to the escalation to ban the offending IP address completely, after many user accounts have been banned.  Set it "On", and set the allowed rate of account lockouts that will trigger escalation, per time period in hours.  The "Fail2Ban jail" setting refers to the fail2ban software's internal configuration that will manage those bans.
  • Note that the mechanism ignores login failures from non-existent users.  Don't be alarmed by repeated password-guessing attacks that don't get blocked, if the user doesn't exist.

Login Failures and Bans -- Future Goal

The mechanism first bans (IP, account) pairs.  Continued abuse results in banning the IP address through the fail2ban mechanism.  Continued abuse results in locking the user account, as a last resort. 

This procedure complements that documentation:

  • Consult policy to figure out how banning should be escalated depending on the failure rates
  • Login to the administrative interface, a.k.a. backend, at /administrator
  • Navigate to Users -> Members -> Options icon (wrench and hammer)
  • In the popup window, go to the tab “Login Settings”
  • "Maximum Failed Login Attempts" refers to specific (IP, account) pair login failures.  Also set the "Time in Hours".
  • "Fail2ban" refers to the escalation to ban the offending IP address completely, after many (IP, account) pairs have been banned.  Set in "On", and set the allowed rate of (IP, account) pair blockage that will trigger escalation, per time period in hours.  The "Fail2Ban jail" setting refers to the fail2ban software's internal configuration that will manage those bans.
  • Further login failures for individual accounts eventually result in a lockout or ban of the account.

 

Password Hashing

Passwords are protected from leaks by hashing them. 

  • As above, navigate to Users -> Members -> Options icon (wrench and hammer)
  • In the popup window, go to the tab “Password”
  • Select SHA-512

Password Complexity (Quality) Change Procedure

Password rules are stored in the database table "jos_password_rule";  the UI modifies this table.  They can specify a "character class", e.g., "alpha" for alphabetic characters.  There are already hard-coded character classes (see list below).  If needed, additional ones can be defined in the table "jos_password_character_class".

  • Consult policy to figure out requirements for the hub in question
  • Login to the administrative interface, a.k.a. backend, at /administrator
  • Navigate to Users -> Members -> Passwords
  • Enable the desired rules
  • To change particular values in a rule, click on the rule's description.  For example, the rule "notReused" can have the duration in days, and the description, changed by clicking on the description "Must be different than the previous password (re-use of the same password will not be allowed for one (1) year)"

Example Rule:

minPasswordLength: Passwords must be at least 8 characters long;  set "Value" to 8

List of predefined (hard-coded) character classes ("Class:" input) when creating a password rule:

  • uppercase:  '[A-Z]'
  • numeric: '[0-9]'
  • lowercase: '[a-z]'
  • special: '[!"\'(),-.:;?[`{}#$%&*+<=>@^_|~\]\/\\\]'
  • nonalpha: '[!"\'(),\-.:;?[`{}#$%&*+<=>@^_|~\]\/\\\0-9]'
  • alpha: '[A-Za-z]'

These are defined in the file core/libraries/Hubzero/Password/CharacterClass.php

title: Commit Messages
content:
GIT commit messages are generally comprised of three sections: a short summary, a longer explanation, and links to references. Starting with this structure forces you to answer why the change is necessary before outlining the changes that you have made.

  • The summary should be no longer than 50 characters
  • The summary should be tagged with what type of commit it is. For example, "[feat] Added a new feature" or "[fix] Fixed a bug".
  • Each line of the explanation should wrap at 72 characters
  • If a commit fixes an issue, it should be denoted with Fixes: {url}
  • If a commit references another commit, outside source, etc, it should be denoted with Refs: {url}

The summary is required but the longer explanation and refs may not always be necessary or apply to the situation at hand.

Template

You can tell GIT to use a template for commit messages with this structure. This is done by setting commit.template in ~/.gitconfig:

[commit]
  template = ~/.gitmessage

Then create ~/.gitmessage with the following:


#-----------------------50-----------------------|
#Summary (50 characters)

#----------------------------------72----------------------------------|
#Explanation (wrap around 72 characters (80 - short indent on either side))

#----------------------------------72----------------------------------|

#----------------------------------72----------------------------------|
#Refs:
#Fixes:
#----------------------------------72----------------------------------|
# Type can be
#    feat     (new feature)
#    fix      (bug fix)
#    refactor (refactoring production code)
#    style    (formatting, missing semi colons, etc; no code change)
#    docs     (changes to documentation)
#    test     (adding or refactoring tests; no production code change)

title: Project File Connectors
content:
Project File Connectors

HUBzero allows for files to be shared either on a repository owned by the Hub or connect to other file management platforms. Project File Connectors allow for these third-party file management systems to enable files uploaded on the Hub yet stored in their system. Follow these instructions to set-up and provide Project File Connectors to your users:

  1. Navigate to the third party file management system of your choosing, such as Google Drive or Dropbox
  2. Set-up either a new project or application and fill in information about the Hub in order to obtain an API key and API secret upon saving
  3. Make sure you set the callback address to your Hub and indicate the appropriate file system
    1. Example: When setting up a Google Drive API connector to redirect to YourHub, the following callback should be used - https://yourhub.org/developer/callback/googledriveAuthorize
  4. Once the API key and API secret have been created successfully, navigate back to the /administrator interface and login
  5. Hover over Extensions and select from the dropdown Plug-in Manager
  6. Search or locate the appropriate plugin connected to the file system
    1. Example: If the file system chosen is Google Drive, one would select the Filesystem - Google Drive plugin
  7. Click on the title of the plugin and change the status to Enabled
  8. Insert the API Key in the Client ID and the API Secret in the Client Secret
  9. Fill in an further information as necessary then click Save & Close
  10. While still at the Plug-in Manager, search for and click the Projects - Files plugin.
  11. Scroll down until you see an option for Default Action, and set it to Connections (view available connections).
  12. Navigate to a Project you would like to setup a new file system
    1. Note: You must be a manager of the Project in order for you to set-up the File System
  13. Click on Files and then click on New Connection and choose the file system from the dropdown
  14. Choose to bypass the secondary step of connecting to the same API..... 

Setting up an External Application (Dropbox, Google Drive, AWS S3)

For using external services via OAuth2 the Hub needs a client identifier and secret for use with that service.  The methods of obtaining these values vary from service to service and are subject to change at the provider's discretion.  Below are the instructions for setting up a developer application on some services (adapting the instructions with some searching should yield similar results for other services or services that have changed their process in the future).

[Creating an application on Dropbox]

  1. Navigate to https://www.dropbox.com/developers
  2. Sign in using the Dropbox credentials that you would like your Hub (the server itself) to authenticate against, this is usually an account owned by the group or organization.
  3. On the left menu, click "My Apps".
  4. On the top right, click "Create App".
  5. Select the access level you would like to grant your Hub to your users Dropbox accounts.
  6. Give the application a name (this name will be displayed to users when they authorize access to their Dropbox account).
  7. Read and agree (or disagree) to Dropbox's terms.
  8. Click "Enable additional users".
  9. In the redirect URIs section, add the URI of "https://<yourhub.org>/developer/callback/dropboxAuthorize".
  10. At this point you should save the "App key" and show and save your "App secret", you will need to input these on cdmHUB in a later step.
  11. You can now click on the branding tab and brand the application to your Hub's needs (adding icons, links to the website, etc.).  These are all used when a user is asked to enter their Dropbox credentials on behalf of your Hub.

Dropbox currently limits development accounts to 500 users per id/key, this can be raised by contacting Dropbox support and applying for a production key once that limit has been reached.

 

[Creating an application on Dropbox]

  1. Log in to your Google account and go to the APIs & services
  2. Navigate to "Credentials" using the left-hand menu 
  3. On the "Credentials" page, click "Create credentials" and choose "OAuth client ID"
  4. Create "New Credentials"
  5. On the "Create client id" page, select "Web application". In the new fields that display, set the following parameters:
    1. Field:   Description
    2. Name:    The name of your web app
    3. Authorized JavaScript origins:   
      1. https://yourhub.org
    4. Authorized redirect URIs:       
      1. https://yourhub.org/projects/auth  
      2. https://yourhub.org/developer/callback/googledriveAuthorize
    5. Web App Credentials: Configuration
  6. Click "Create" to proceed
    1. Your "Client Id" and "Client Secret" will be displayed
  7. Save your Client Id and Client Secret to enter into the Connection settings into "Filesystems - Google Drive" plugin
    1. Additional documentation can be found here: 
      1. https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/api-keys

title: Dataviewer:  Databases within Projects
content:
Databases within projects are also known as "dataviewer".  This is a plugin called "Projects - Databases".  This software uses different database users, one to write, and one to view data. 

Setting up dataviewer

 

# /usr/bin/hzcms configure dataviewer --enable
enabling dataviewer
creating database user: dataviewer, password = ...
creating database user: datawriter, password = ...

 

The above should setup the passwords also, which can be verified by looking at  /administrator -> Plug-in Manager: Plug-ins -> Projects - Databases

This should do something equivalent to: 

function generate() {
  openssl rand -base64 15
}

function rand_alnum() {
  generate | sed 's/[^a-zA-Z0-9]//g' | cut -c1-16
}

MYSQL_PASS_VIEW=`rand_alnum`
MYSQL_PASS_WRITE=`rand_alnum`

echo run the echoed statements below in MySQL and copy the passwords into Plug-in Manager: Databases
echo "GRANT USAGE ON *.* TO 'dataviewer'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY '$MYSQL_PASS_VIEW';"
echo "GRANT SELECT ON `prj_db_%`.* TO 'dataviewer'@'localhost';"

echo "GRANT USAGE ON *.* TO 'datawriter'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY '$MYSQL_PASS_WRITE';"
echo "GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, DROP ON `prj_db_%`.* TO 'datawriter'@'localhost';"

echo "flush privileges;"

 

Symptoms that this needs to be setup:

Log entries in /var/log/syslog like:

Sep 22 11:32:14 dev.qubeshub.org mysqld: 170922 11:32:14 [Warning] Access denied for user 'datawriter'@'localhost' (using password: YES)
