title: Solr Configuration
content:
The most up-to-date repository for hubzero-solr is located at gitolite@help.hubzero.org:hubzero/hubzero-solr

Overview

Apache Solr is an open-source, mature, and stable searching service that is built upon the Apache Lucene search engine. The service provides features which lend itself to scaling and has a rich open source community. It is a Java-based service which provides search results through HTTP. Many companies such as Instagram, eBay, and StubHub rely on Solr to provide advanced searching capabilities.

The HUBzero Development Team is working to “integrate not reinvent” services which are beneficial to the user base. Searching and finding relevant content is not an easy task when access controls, non-normalized, user data is involved. Over the years, several attempts to provide a successful searching experience has proved to be challenging. In this iteration search stability and flexibility are the overall goals of the HUBzero Solr Integration.

This is a guide for several audiences: Hub Managers, Hub Users, Developers, System Administrators, and Community Managers.

The Solr integration is under active development. Features will be rolled out incrementally and included in future releases moving forward.

User Instructions

Search is available in the top-right of most templates and at https://<hub>/search. Currently, search understands Solr’s default Query Syntax meaning you can perform powerful searches using advanced keywords.

Basic searching: Albert Einstein - results would include matches for “Albert” and “Einstein”. If you enter Al, search would only return results matching AL.

Exact Phrase: “Albert Einstein” - results would include matches for “Albert Einstein”.

Fuzzy Searching: “Al*” - results would include matches for “Al”, “Albert”, “all”, “ally”. This query searches for all results matching the letters A and L.

Tag Searching: tags:”tag phrase” - all results which have the “tag phrase” as the tag.

Title Searching: title: “To Kill a Mockingbird” - results include all matches for content that has the title To Kill a Mockingbird

Author Searching: author: “J.K. Rowling” - results include matches for content that has J.K. Rowling listed as the author.

DOI Searching: doi:10.4231/R76D5QXB - results includes matches with the DOI specified.

Subtractive Searching: -cats - results do not include “cats”.

Additive Searching: +dogs - results include and favor matching “dogs”.

What's currently searchable?

The HUBzero Development team is incrementally rolling out support for the various types of content. At this time, the following areas are searchable:

  • Resources

  • Publications

  • Citations

  • Projects

  • Groups

  • Members

  • Content Pages

  • Knowledge Base Articles

Hub Manager Instructions

Those who have access to the hub administrative backend can perform a couple of a tasks which can change the behavior of Search across the hub. This is a brief walk-through of some of those capabilities.

Search Overview Page

The Search Overview Page is a quick health monitor for the search service. When search is properly configured the Search Overview Page should show a green check mark and indicated that the search engine is responding. The “last insert” should reflect that an update has occurred no more than 30 minutes ago.

Troubleshooting Tip: If the time the “last insert” exceeds 30 minutes, check to see if the Hub’s cron is running. A System Administrator should verify that the task in /etc/cron.d/cron-hzsolrindex is executing appropriately. The System Administrator should run hzsolrindex manually to see if there are any errors.

If the HUBzero CMS cannot make a connection to the Solr search engine, the following screen may appear indicating an error.

Troubleshooting Tip: If this screen appears, verify that the Solr search engine is running. A system administrator may need to run service hubzero-solr restart or /etc/init.d/hubzero-solr restart. Also verify that the configuration is correct according to the installation notes.

Search Index

The search index view shows the default facets or categories for search. These are created by default and should NOT be removed or edited. They are the fundamental types that search knows about.

 

Custom Facets

A hub manager may get the request to have a special category under Resources called “Learning Materials” which are all resources that have been tagged with “learning resource”. From the Search Overview Page, the manager would click the “+” new item and fill out the New Facet form as shown below, making sure to Save and Close the form when finished.

 

Indexed Documents

On the search overview page, the count of matching documents is displayed for each category. If you click the number under Count, you will be taken to matching document view.

The indexed documents view gives the hub manager an opportunity to spot-check results. They can use the Filter bar at the top to further narrow the listing of matching documents.

 

Removing Trashed Articles (404)

On the backend: Article manager -> find the article by alias -> goto trashed to find it -> take note of ID

On the backend: Components -> Search -> (Category) -> Search for ID in previous step -> Add to Blacklist

 

Blacklist

Let’s say the Hub Manager notices a few entries which are spammy and they want to remove them from all user’s search results. Clicking the “Add to Blacklist” button will immediately delete the search result and prevent the entry from being re-indexed. The record will be placed on the blacklist. If the manager wishes to have the item re-indexed, they can click the “Remove Entry” from the Index Blacklist view. The entry will be re-indexed the next time hzsolrindex is called by the system.

Administrators will have the ability to remove entries from the front-end. Clicking the trashcan icon will immediately remove the search entry and add it to the blacklist. The blacklist is manageable from the administrative backend.

Successful removal of the entry will produce the following message.

 

Installation

The installation of the Solr requires the installation of the hubzero-solr package via your distribution’s package manager - yum or apt for HUBzero supported distributions. For information on how to setup your repository please refer to the HUBzero installation documentation.

These instructions assume you have privileged access to a terminal on the HUBzero Web Server. If you do not, you will need a System Administrator to assist with some steps in this configuration.

 

Requirements

For Solr to run properly, we assume that your system meets the production HUB requirements. The initialization of the Solr service may require at least 2GB of memory. The Solr integration is made available through code contained in the HUBzero 2.1.6 release, so you will need at least version 2.1.6.

 

Quick Start

  1. Install the hubzero-solr package via yum or aptitude on the HUBzero Web Server.

    1. This creates the hubzero-solr user.

    2. This installs /etc/cron.d/cron-hzsolrindex CRON task to run every 30 minutes on the top of the hour and the ½ hour.

    3. This installs Solr in /srv/hubzero-solr

  2. On the HUBzero Web Server: touch /var/log/hzsolrindex.log && chown hubzero-solr:hubzero-solr /var/log/hzsolrindex.log

    1. This will be fixed in an upcoming package update.

  3. Go to the Administrative Backend, go to Components >> Search.

  4. Go to the Search Options.

  5. Under the Search Manager Options Window, click the Solr tab.

  6. Ensure the settings match your configuration. HUBzero Production hubs use values different than the default configuration. Open Source hubs should not need to deviate from the default values.

  7. Click the Defaults tab under the Search Manager Options Window.

  8. Switch the Search Engine from "Basic" to "Apache Solr"

Developer Notes

In order to maintain and develop new functionality, here are some details which may be useful to know. This documentation assumes the reader has a mid-range to advanced knowledge of the following topics: PHP, Python, Linux System Administration, HTTP RESTful APIs, NoSQL Document Stores.

Architecture

The HUBzero Solr Integration is comprised of a couple of components that are loosely bound. The HUBzero Solr installation includes Apache Solr, an indexing script called hzsolrindex, the cron-hzsolrindex CRON task, and the CMS’s API.

Apache Solr

The Apache Solr service is comprises of an HTTP API, an administrator interface, and a background worker to process requests and analyze search data. It uses Jetty and Apache Lucene on the backend. At the time of writing, we are using version Apache Solr version 6.1.0. Apache Solr has the ability to keep track of different indices called “cores” in Solr-speak. A core consists of a data directory, which is a filesystem representation of the document store and a config directory which is home to a surprising number of tunable configuration options in XML format.

hzsolrindex

The Python script hzsolrindex is located in /usr/bin/hzsolrindex. It is a script which pages through the api in the Supported Search Areas. At this time it is only capable of running a full index operation, meaning that all information is crawled each time the application is invoked. The script was written to use standard Python libraries or those that are already included by the hubzero-python or hubzero-cli packages.

 

hzsolrindex relies on a couple files to make assumptions about its environment:

  • /etc/hubzero.conf

    • Default site - used to know which hub to operate on.

    • uri - used to know where to crawl the API.

    • Hubdir - used to find where the app/config/solr.json is.

  • app/config/solr.json

    • Application_id: which API application to use to get a token.

    • Application_secret: application’s secret, used for getting a token.

    • Solr_username: Name of the user which is created for hzsolrindex to use to crawl the API.

    • Solr_password: password of the hubzerosolrworker CMS user.

    • Solr_port: the port the Solr service is running on.

    • Solr_host: the host which solr is running on (more likely locahost)

cron-hzsolrindex

A simple CRON task is installed by the hubzero-solr package in /etc/cron.d/cron-hzsolrindex. It contains the following line:

0,30 * * * * hubzero-solr umask 077; /usr/bin/hzsolrindex 2>&1 >> /var/log/hzsolrindex.log

Troubleshooting Tip: If the CRON job is not running, check to see if the hubzero-solr user can write to the /var/log/hzsolrindex.log file. The hubzero-solr user and the hubzero-solr group should own the file. Permissions on this file should be 644. A simple test would be to run the CRON command as the hubzero-solr user to make sure everything works.

  1. sudo su -s /bin/bash hubzero-solr

  2. umask 077; /usr/bin/hzsolrindex 2>&1 >>  /var/log/hzsolrindex.log

HUBzero CMS

The hubzero-cms version 2.1.6 contains the necessary code for Solr to work properly. The com_search/admin/controllers/solr.php controller contains an execute() method which checks for the existence of <hubdir>/app/config/solr.json. If that file is not present, a couple of things happen:

  • CMS HUBzero Solr Worker Created

  • CMS API Application Created

  • Creation of solr.json in app/config

 

Solr.json is used by hzsolrindex to know how to talk about to the CMS and Solr.

 

Plg_search_solr exists to be triggered anytime a Relational model save() method is called. This is currently a placeholder. There is an Event::trigger() in the Relational class right now and the plugin is triggered, but there is no logic to do anything at this time. This may be deprecated if we implement a queuing system.

 

The API has been extended to react to a ‘searchable’ parameter. If the API user is an admin and they pass ‘searchable’ to the endpoint, the returned document will be modified to match the Solr Document format. I propose that in future version of the API we formalize a format to return and build it into the API application.

Purging the Index

Sometimes bad data gets index and you want to start fresh. On the command-line of the hub in which you would like to purge the index run the following curl command. The double-quotes are needed.

curl -v -L "http://localhost:8445/solr/hubzero-solr-core/update?commit=true&stream.body=%3Cdelete%3E%3Cquery%3E*:*%3C/query%3E%3C/delete%3E"

You may have to change port 8445 to something different!

 

Hosted Hub Port Scheme

Due to the HUBzero virtualized hub configuration, many hubs may exist on a single host. The following scheme is designed to prevent conflicts between the Solr services running in the different environments.

Host Port
qa 2092
stage 2091
dev 2090
production 2093
open source 8445

 

 

Suggestions and Future Work

At the time of writing, there is still a lot of work needed to continue making Solr Search useful to the end user.

Known Issues:

  • Infinite loop in hzsolrindex when indexing an empty hub.

    • Need to adjust the pagination check.

 

  • Formatting issues with some results which have HTML or template placeholders in them.

    • {{2}[^s]+}{2}

 

  • Exceedingly long strings entered into the search box will return an error code from Apache “Request too Long”.

    • Truncate requests?

    • May be alleviated once view is converted to JS?

  • Tags on Member Profiles are not recognized as tags.

  • Possible formatting issues with Member Profile?

    • JSON blob instead of profile information.

Search Coverage:

  • Index Project Files

  • Index Group Content

    • Store in raw_content field of group

    • Create new hubtypes?

  • Index Collections

  • Index Events

  • Index Forums

  • Index Blogs

  • Index Wishes

  • Index Documentation

  • Index Support Tickets

  • Index Newsletters

Suggestions:

  • Adapt hzsolrindex to listen to RabbitMQ for additions, updates, or removals.

  • Increase error logging in hzsolrindex

  • Clean up hzsolrindex: each API endpoint code may be redundant.

  • Increase the frequency of when hzsolrindex is invoked, this would mean that it shouldn’t completely rebuild the index every time.

Features:

  • Suggest as you type.

  • Did you mean?

  • Better highlighting.

  • Selective indexing.

    • Turn off certain categories.

      • Could be implemented with a filter, right now.

  • Interface: Filtering

    • My Stuff

    • Groups

  • Embeddable Search Module.

    • Filters applied to module

    • Use-case: StemedHub Group Resources

title: Server
content:
Overview

Hubzero\Content\Server object serve up files as download.

This allows for simple but smart objects with get and set methods and an internal error handler

Usage

Set the filename
filename(string filename = null) : mixed

Return: String filename if field is set, NULL if not

 

Set the disposition value
disposition(string $disposition = null) : mixed

Return: String value of disposition if field is set, NULL if not

$disposition:

  • 'inline': Read the contents of a file and display it inline (display in browser window)
  • 'attachment': Read the contents of a file and display as attachment (browser should default to saving file rather than displaying)

 

Set the name to save file as
saveas(string $saveas = null) : mixed

Return: String name of the file if field is set, NULL if not

$saveas: name to save file as

 

Read the contents of a file and display it
serve() : boolean

Example

$server = new Hubzero\Content\Server;
$server->filename(PATH_APP . '/site/media/patch.txt');
$server->disposition('attachment');
$server->saveas('bugfix.patch');
$server->serve();

title: Fail2Ban - CMS
content:
Fail2Ban Integration

 

HUBzero CMS Authentication

Fail2Ban Integration

 

 

Objective

CMS Configuration Page

User Password Reset Limit

User Failed Login Limit

IP-based Blocked User Limit

Assumptions

Setup & Configuration

sudo Configuration

Fail2Ban Configuration

[Sample] Jail Configuration

[Sample] Filter Configuration

[Sample] Action Configuration

[Sample] Banned IP address results

Developer Commentary

User Impact

Objective

To have the CMS handle user login banning in an attempt to deter brute force attacks.

CMS Configuration Page

The following settings are accessible from the CMS administrative backend.

These options are accessible by going to the User Menu - Members and Member Options.

User Password Reset Limit

The number of password resets per time period is limited. If the user attempts to reset their password at a threshold deemed by the HUB administrator as excessive, the following message is displayed.

 

 

 

 

User Failed Login Limit

The number of failed logins per time period is limited. If the user attempts to reset their password at a threshold deemed by the HUB administrator as excessive, the following message is displayed. This means that an individual's account is temporarily blocked until the time period expires.

IP-based Blocked User Limit

When the threshold of blocked user accounts per IP network is met, the CMS will trigger a Fail2Ban rule which will block incoming requests from an IP address for a period of time. This is the last line of defense as blocking an IP address may have unintended consequences - such as blocking a NAT-ed IP address which several valid users are using to access the hub.

Assumptions

This approach assumes that the system administrator has configured a jail and a system user account to execute (with sudo) Fail2Ban via the fail2ban-client utility.

 

On Debian Hosts, Fail2Ban should be version 0.9.5.
0.9.5-1~nd70+1 from http://neuro.debian.net/debian/ wheezy/main amd64 Packages

 

 

Setup & Configuration

There are a number of subsystems which need to be configured for this scheme to work properly.

sudo Configuration

A privileged user which can execute:

   (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/fail2ban-client set hub-login banip [0-9.]*

   (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/fail2ban-client set hub-login unbanip [0-9.]*

 

This can be accomplished by adding a sudoers rule in /etc/sudoers.d/ that looks like:

www-data  ALL=(root)NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/fail2ban-client set hub-login banip [0-9.]*

Fail2Ban Configuration

The system administrator should configure Fail2Ban to create jails which the CMS can add offending IP address into. The amount of time that the ban is valid is configured in Fail2Ban.

 

The CMS will simply add IP addresses to the Fail2Ban jail which will trigger the Ban Action as specified in the rule set.

 

The following configuration are more of an example than anything. A seasoned system administrator will have crafted better rules.

[Sample] Jail Configuration

#

# JAILS

# /etc/fail2ban/jail.local

#

[hub-login]

enabled  = true

port     = http,https

filter   = hub-login

logpath  = /var/log/messages

banaction = hublogin-failure

bantime = 600

findtime = 1

maxretry = 1

 

[Sample] Filter Configuration

/etc/fail2ban/filter.d/hub-login.conf

# Fail2Ban configuration file

#

[Definition]

 

 

# Option:  failregex

# Notes.:  Regexp to catch known spambots and software alike. Please verify

#          that it is your intent to block IPs which were driven by

#          abovementioned bots.

# Values:  TEXT

#

 

#We choose something that will never happen

# Since the CMS will control IP’s placed in the jails

failregex = ^<HOST>thisfilterwillneverbefound

 

# Option:  ignoreregex

# Notes.:  regex to ignore. If this regex matches, the line is ignored.

# Values:  TEXT

#

ignoreregex =

 

[Sample] Action Configuration

# Fail2Ban configuration file

# cat /etc/fail2ban/action.d/hublogin-failure.conf

 

[INCLUDES]

 

before = iptables-common.conf


[Definition]

 

# Option:  actionstart

# Notes.:  command executed once at the start of Fail2Ban.

# Values:  CMD

#

actionstart = iptables -N fail2ban-hublogin

             iptables -A INPUT -j DROP

             iptables -I INPUT -p tcp -j fail2ban-hublogin

 

# Option:  actionstop

# Notes.:  command executed once at the end of Fail2Ban

# Values:  CMD

#

actionstop = iptables -D fail2ban-hublogin -p tcp -j fail2ban-hublogin

            iptables -F fail2ban-hublogin

            iptables -X fail2ban-hublogin

 

# Option:  actioncheck

# Notes.:  command executed once before each actionban command

# Values:  CMD

#

actioncheck = iptables -n -L fail2ban-hublogin | grep -q fail2ban-hublogin

 

# Option:  actionban

# Notes.:  command executed when banning an IP. Take care that the

#          command is executed with Fail2Ban user rights.

# Tags:    <ip>  IP address

#          <failures>  number of failures

#          <time>  unix timestamp of the ban time

# Values:  CMD

#

actionban = iptables -I fail2ban-hublogin -p tcp --dport 443 -s <ip> -j DROP

iptables -I fail2ban-hublogin -p tcp --dport 80 -s <ip> -j DROP

 

# Option:  actionunban

# Notes.:  command executed when unbanning an IP. Take care that the

#          command is executed with Fail2Ban user rights.

# Tags:    <ip>  IP address

#          <failures>  number of failures

#          <time>  unix timestamp of the ban time

# Values:  CMD

#

actionunban = iptables -D fail2ban-hublogin -p tcp --dport 443 -s <ip> -j DROP

iptables -D fail2ban-hublogin -p tcp --dport 80 -s <ip> -j DROP

 

[Init]

 

# Defaut name of the chain

#

name = DEFAULT

 

# Option:  protocol

# Notes.:  internally used by config reader for interpolations.

# Values:  [ tcp | udp | icmp | all ] Default: tcp

#

protocol = tcp

 

# Option:  chain

# Notes    specifies the iptables chain to which the fail2ban rules should be

#          added

chain = INPUT

Developer Commentary

This feature has been designed primarily with HUBzero’s production environment in mind. While it would be nice to implement a generalized feature set for all distributions, it simply is not within the scope of this undertaking. This feature should be revisited frequently to determine whether or not it is appropriate to keep within the code base - or implemented as a plugin. I chose not to implement this as a plugin as I did not necessarily see the need to separate this from the HUBzero Authentication Plugin as it’s the only vector which is vulnerable to brute-force attacks which we have direct control over.

User Impact

When a large number of people intend on using the CMS, it may be wise to temporarily disable this feature (e.g. conference, class activity, etc). In the past, many conference goers have mistyped their password in a short period of time creating a false positive for normal Fail2Ban operation. This risk is mitigated by the fact that the number of blocked users is observed before triggering Fail2Ban.

 

This can be accomplished by turning this check off by going to the /administrator -> Members -> Member Options -> Login Settings -> Fail2Ban set to “Off”.

 

This implementation should give HUB owners more flexibility over their settings.

title: Redirect
content:
Overview

App::redirect helps you to redirect current request to a new request or sub-request.

Usage

App::redirect(string $url, string $message = null, string $type = 'success')

Params

$url is the url to redirect to.

$message is the message to display on redirect. (Default value => null)

$type is the message type. (Default value => 'success')

Application

Situation

What if a user is logged out, but the user sends a request which needs an authorization?

Solution

We need to notify the users that they are logged out and send a page to let them log in first. Then they can access to their request.

Code

// Check if user is logged in
if (User::isGuest())
{
    // Store the request uri
    $return = base64_encode($_SERVER['REQUEST_URI']);
    // Require login and recall back if seccess
    App::redirect(
        Route::url('index.php?option=com_users&view=login&return=' . $return),
        'Please login to continue',
        'warning'
    );
}

title: CMS Extensions
content:
Overview

HUBzero CMS is already a rich featured content management system but if you're building a hub and you need extra features which aren't available by default, you can easily extend it with extensions. There are five types of extensions: Components, Modules, Plugins, Templates, and Languages. Each of these extensions handle specific functionality.

Components

The largest and most complex of the extension types, a component is in fact a separate application. You can think of a component as something that has its own functionality, its own database tables and its own presentation. So if you install a component, you add an application to your website. Examples of components are a forum, a blog, a community system, a photo gallery, etc. You could think of all of these as being a separate application. Everyone of these would make perfectly sense as a stand-alone system. A component will be shown in the main part of your website and only one component will be shown. A menu is then in fact nothing more then a switch between different components.

Modules

Modules are extensions which present certain pieces of information on your site. It's a way of presenting information that is already present. This can add a new function to an application which was already part of your website. Think about latest article modules, login module, a menu, etc. Typically you'll have a number of modules on each web page. The difference between a module and a component is not always very clear for everybody. A module doesn't make sense as a standalone application, it will just present information or add a function to an existing application. Take a newsletter for instance. A newsletter is a module. You can have a website which is used as a newsletter only. That makes perfectly sense. Although a newsletter module probably will have a subscription page integrated, you might want to add a subscription module on a sidebar on every page of your website. You can put this subscribe module anywhere on your site.

Another commonly used module would be a search box you wish to be present throughout your site. This is a small piece of re-usable HTML that can be placed anywhere you like and in different locations on a template-by-template basis. This allows one site to have the module in the top left of their template, for instance, and another site to have it in the right side-bar.

Plugins

Plugins serve a variety of purposes. As modules enhance the presentation of the final output of the Web site, plugins enhance the data and can also provide additional, installable functionality. Plugins enable you to execute code in response to certain events, either core events or custom events that are triggered from your own code. This is a powerful way of extending the basic functionality.

Templates

A template is a series of files within the Joomla! CMS that control the presentation of the content. The template is not a website; it's also not considered a complete website design. The template is the basic foundation design for viewing your website. To produce the effect of a "complete" website, the template works hand-in-hand with the content stored in the database.

Each hub comes with default templates for both the administrator area and the front-end site.

Languages

Probably the most basic extensions are languages. Languages can be packaged in two ways, either as a core package or as an extension package. In essence, these files consist key/value pairs, these pairs provide the translation of static text strings which are assigned within the source code. These language packs will affect both the front and administrator side. Note: these language packs also include an XML meta file which describes the language and font information to use for PDF content generation.

Conclusion

If the difference between the three types of extensions is still not completely clear, then it is advisable to go to the admin pages of your installation and check the components menu, the module manager and the plugin manager. A hub comes with a number of core components, modules and plugins. By checking what they're doing, the difference between the three types of building blocks should become clear.

content:

title: Hub Users
content:
A hub is a single community place for your colleagues, peers, and collaborators. Your community will interact with the HUBzero® platform through the user interface, enabling access to analytical tools, publishing data, sharing resources, collaborating, and building community spaces.

  • How to create an account on a hub
  • Filling out your member profile
  • Customizing your member dashboard

 

 

Every HUBzero® platform offers the following core features. 

Run Applications

Every instance of HUBzero® has the ability for online applications, otherwise known as "tools," to be hosted on the hub. These interactive computations and analytical tools can use Linux, Jupyter, RStudio, and other Web Applications. 
 
The process starts with a member filling out a web form to register their intent to submit a tool. The member then uploads code into a subversion source code repository and develops the code within a workspace. The member can work alone or with their team to build the tool and design a graphical user interface. With a little help from the managers of the hub, tools can be installed and published for either a limited group of colleagues or for the entire community. 
 

Collaborate 

HUBzero® instances provide multiple spaces for research teams and collaborators to discuss data concepts, track progress and share files by using the services you already know, such as Google Drive, GitHub, or Dropbox.

 

Groups

Groups are an easy way to share content and conversation, either privately or with the world. Each group comes with the ability to create group-specific content pages, invite and manage group membership, send announcements, publish a blog, add events through a calendar, share ideas through collections, discuss methods through forums, work on tasks through projects, share information through wikis, manage files, and much more. 

Projects

Whether working on a new funding proposal, research paper or developing an application, projects are a great way to manage your data, workflow, and communication. Each project space comes with a wiki area, to-do list management, the ability to connect to Google Drive, Dropbox and other file management systems, and publishing data straight from a project space.

Wiki

Wiki pages are user-written articles on a range of subjects. Any contributor or a group of contributors can create new articles, and there can be multiple articles on the same wiki, each written by a different author. Any member can create a new article. When creating a new article, the initial contributor can choose to have a defined list of authors, all of whom can edit the page, or have an open, wiki-like format where anyone can contribute.

Collections

A quick and easy way to share, favorite, and organize information on a hub. Start with an image, link, or file you would like to share with your community. Share the collected content in a post by uploading the materials or collecting the materials from around the hub. Fellow community members can collect and follow your collections and individual posts, which allows for any updates to appear in their collection feed. 

Publish

HUBzero® offers several ways to publish information on a hub. Step–by–step guided systems walk you through publishing research products, including datasets and white papers. All research can be published with a minted DOI, a license, and an opportunity for peer review.

While most publishing features come with predefined categories, administrators can manage categories and master types through a configuration interface along with adding new licenses, batch creates materials, and administer all drafted to published versions of data.

Publications

Contributors are guided through the publishing process in easy, manageable steps. Whether uploading files, writing an abstract, or managing authorship, the member is always kept up-to-date on what has been done and what's left to do. Every step can be re-visited at a later time, allowing members to work at their own pace.

Curation

Site members can be designated as curators to ensure quality content before final publishing. Curators can review all the parts of the publication and make notes on areas of improvement before the publication is officially published. Curation helps ensure your visitors are treated to the highest caliber content.

title: CMS-Controlled Fail2Ban Jail
content:
Configuration and Details

Objective

To have the CMS handle user login banning in an attempt to deter brute force attacks.

 

CMS Configuration Page

The following settings are accessible from the CMS administrative backend.

These options are accessible by going to the User Menu ­ Members and Member Options.

User Password Reset Limit

The number of password resets per time period is limited. If the user attempts to reset their password at a threshold deemed by the HUB administrator as excessive, the following message is displayed.

User Failed Login Limit

The number of failed logins per time period is limited. If the user attempts to reset their password at a threshold deemed by the HUB administrator as excessive, the following message is displayed. This means that an individual's account is temporarily blocked until the time period expires.

IP­based Blocked User Limit

When the threshold of blocked user accounts per IP network is met, the CMS will trigger a Fail2Ban rule which will block incoming requests from an IP address for a period of time. This is the last line of defense as blocking an IP address may have unintended consequences ­ such as blocking a NAT­ed IP address which several valid users are using to access the hub.

 

Assumptions

This approach assumes that the system administrator has configured a jail and a system user account to execute (with sudo) Fail2Ban via the fail2ban­client utility.

 

On Debian Hosts, Fail2Ban should be version 0.9.5.

0.9.5­1~nd70+1 from http://neuro.debian.net/debian/ wheezy/main amd64 Packages

title: Development Environment
content:
Setting up your Development Environment

The HUBzero Platform is comprised of many software packages woven together into an a single system. The minimum requirements for developing HUBzero web code can be a simple Linux Apache MySQL PHP (LAMP) server matching the currently supported Linux distribution. At the time of writing, Centos 7. Although the a simple LAMP server should suffice, it should not The HUBzero maintainers try to ensure that system administrators do not have to deviate too much from the stock distribution in order to install HUBzero.

Setup Development Environment via VMware Image

The Hubzero maintainers package a VMware Image available for evaluation and development purposes available for download at https://hubzero.org/download.

Setup Development Environment via Packages

If you are confident in your Linux system administration skills, the Hub can be built via Debian and RedHat packages. Instructions can be found in our documentation under System Administrators. Once the hub is operational, you will want to clone the hubzero-cms repository for development.

See the Getting the Latest Code section for instructions on how to use git to grab the latest code.

 

Getting the Latest Code

In the pre-packaged development environments listed above, the hubzero-cms code is a snapshot of when the package was created. To obtain the latest code, we will use git to clone the hubzero-cms repository.

In order to get the latest code you will need:

  • SSH access to the machine
  • sudo privileges 
  • git

A couple conventions for this section, in particular:

  • this text indicates an incantation to be typed in the terminal.
  • <something> indicates something that should be replaced with value you have set.
  • [!] indicates something that should be interpreted, or have your judgment applied.
     
  1. ssh <username>@<hostname>
    1. Log into your development server
  2. cd /var/www [!]
    1. Change into the webroot directory.
    2. [!]: This may be /www in some configurations.
  3. mv <hubname> <hubname>.bak [!]
    1. Backup the existing hubzero-cms installation.
    2. [!]: The name of the directory may change depending on what <hubname> is used for hzcms install. In the documentation, 'example' is used. Therefore the directory will be /var/www/example.
  4. git clone https://github.com/hubzero/hubzero.git <hubname>
    1. This will clone the latest release into your webroot.  The 'dev' branch is the default.  You may switch to another available at this step if desired.
    2. This will create the shell of the application, we will need to (re)-populate it with configuration values and pull in external dependencies later on.
  5. cp <hubname>.bak/app <hubname>/.
    1. This moves the configuration files back into the application.  If prompted, overwrite the new app/ directory.
  6. cd <hubname>/core
    1. Navigate to the core directory.
  7. php ./bin/composer install
    1. Pull in external dependencies using composer.
  8. cd ../
    1. Navigate back to the /var/www/<hubname> directory.
  9. php muse migration -i -f
    1. Run database migrations. This helps maintain the database's schema between versions.  Note: Reversing database schema changes can be extremely difficult if needed.
  10. cd /var/www
    1. Navigate back to the directory containing the hub installation.
  11. chown apache:apache <hubname> -R [!]
    1. Change the owner and the group of the hub installation directory. 
    2. [!] The user may be apache OR www-data, depending on the distribution.
  12. chmod 775 <hubname> -R
    1. Change the file permissions to allow the group to read and write permissions.
  13. sudo usermod -aG apache <username>
    1. Add your user to the apache group.
  14. git pull --rebase
    1. Pull the latest code. This should be done periodically.
    2. Use the rebase flag if you already have some commits that you haven't pushed yet. This puts your work on top of the changes that come downstream.

Note: [!] The permissions scheme used here is NOT production safe. It's used for development purposes. File permissions and your security scheme depend on your needs.

title: Apache HTTP Server
content:
Install Apache HTTP Server

The full HUBzero® Platform currently requires Apache HTTP Server 2.4.x. The basic HUBzero CMS product available here should work with any web server that can be configured to run PHP applications (such as Nginx), but will be limited in what additional HUBzero Platform components can be added later.

$ sudo systemctl enable --now httpd

title: MariaDB Community Server
content:
MariaDB Community Server Installation

The full HUBzero® Platform currently requires MariaDB Community Server 10.11.x. The basic HUBzero CMS product available here should work with any database server based on MySQL 5.6 (MySQL, Percona, etc), but will be limited in what additional HUBzero Platform components can be added later.

$ sudo dnf module install mariadb:10.11

title: Linux
content:
Obtain Linux Hosting

The full HUBzero® Platform currently requires Rocky Linux 8. The basic HUBzero CMS product available here should work on any current Linux distribution, but will be limited in what additional HUBzero Platform components can be added later.

Minimum System Requirements

HUBzero Platform installations require one or more dedicated hosts running Rocky Linux 8 (or other Red Hat 8 based distribution). A typical starter HUBzero Platform installation might consist of a single physical server with dual 64-bit quad-core CPUs, 24 Gigabytes of RAM and a terabyte of disk.

Production systems should try to not limit hardware resources, HUBzero Platform is designed to run on systems with many CPU cores and lots of RAM. If you are looking for a system to run a small site with limited physical or virtual resources this is probably not the system for you. However, for demonstration or development purposes we often create VM images with less than a gigabyte of RAM and 5 gigabytes of disk. While fully functional, these virtual machines would only be suitable for a single user doing development or testing.

title: Installation
content:
Target Audience

This document and the installation and maintenance of a HUBzero system has a target audience of experienced Linux administrators (preferably experienced with Enterprise Linux (RedHat/CentOS/Rocky/etc distributions).

Minimum System Requirements

HUBzero (EL) installations require one or more dedicated hosts running Enterprise Linux 8 (RedHat/CentOS/Rocky). Rocky 8 is currently the preferred distribution.

A typical starter HUBzero installation might consist of a single physical server with dual 64-bit quad-core CPUs, 24 Gigabytes of RAM and a terabyte of disk.

Production systems should try to not limit hardware resources, HUBzero is designed to run on systems with many CPU cores and lots of RAM. If you are looking for a system to run a small site with limited physical or virtual resources this is probably not the system for you. However, for demonstration or development purposes we often create VM images with less than a gigabyte of RAM and 5 gigabytes of disk. While fully functional, these virtual machines would only be suitable for a single user doing development or testing.

System Architecture

All hardware, filesystem partitions, RAID configurations, backup models, security models, etc. and base configurations of the hosts email server, SSH server, network, etc. are the responsibility of the system administrator managing the host.

The Hubzero software expects to be installed on a headless server from a minimal ISO.

title: Plugins
content:
Introduction - What is a plugin?


A software component that adds a specific feature to an existing section of the HUB. By allowing plugins to exist the HUB becomes more pliable and flexible to the needs of different users and different functionalities that are not needed in the basic version of the component. Hooks on events.

Supported Plugins

Antispam – Black List: This is a Spam Detector that detects black-listed words. Only flags new content – this plugin is not retroactive.

Antispam – Link Rife: This is a Spam Detector that detects link frequency in a body of text. Has a link to text ratio that can be set. Only flags new content – this plugin is not retroactive.

Antispam – Bayesian Filter: This is a Spam Detector that employs a basic Bayesian filter. Recursive Bayesian estimation that can be trained based on what is flagged as spam (Hubzero Abuse Reports). The more content you train it with, the better the plugin will preform. Only flags new content – this plugin is not retroactive.

Antispam – Baba Ji Spam Detector: Developed by Hubzero to counteract the Baba Ji specific spammer. Only flags new content – this plugin is not retroactive.

Antispam – Akismet: A third party spam detecting service. Has a limit of 5,000 posts a day for a free service. If a Hub goes over that limit then the plugin starts flagging all new content as false, which causes submit problems. Only flags new content – this plugin is not retroactive.

Antispam – Mollom: This plugin uses the remote Mollom service to scan posted content and determine is content has a high probability of being spam or not. Only flags new content – this plugin is not retroactive.

Antispam – SpamAssassin: This plugin scans posted content with SpamAssassin to determine is content has a high probability of being spam or not. This service was developed for email. Only flags new content – this plugin is not retroactive.

Authentication – Hubzero: Handles HUBzero default user authentication. Can send emails to administrators when a new account is created.

Authentication – Facebook: Handles user authentication against Facebook. Does not set a local password.

Authentication – Google: Handles user authentication against Google. Does not set a local password.

Authentication – Linkedin: Handles user authentication against LinkedIn. Does not set a local password.

Authentication – Pucas: Handles user authentication against Purdue's CAS. Does not set a local password.

Authentication – Twitter: Handles user authentication against Twitter. Does not set a local password.

Authentication _ Certificate: Handles user authentication against client side SSL certificates. Does not set a local password.

Authentication – ORCID: Handles user authentication against ORCID. Does not set a local password.

Authentication – Shibboleth: Handles user authentication with Shibboleth/InCommon. Does not set a local password.

Authfactors – Certificate: Alternative to “Authfactors – Certificate”. Handles using a client SSL cert as a secondary auth factor. Does not set a local password.

Authfactors – Authy: Alternative to “Authfactors – Certificate”. Handles using the Authy service as a secondary auth factor. Does not set a local password.

Captcha – ReCaptcha: This CAPTCHA plugin uses the reCAPTCHA service to prevent spammers while it helps to digitize books, newspapers and old radio shows. To get a public and private key for your domain, go to http://www.google.com/recaptcha. To use this for new account registration, go to Options in the User Manager and select Captcha - reCaptcha as the Captcha.

Captcha – Math: A simpler captcha service that uses an math equation to prevent spam bots. It is suggested to use “Captcha – ReCaptcha”.

Captcha – Image: A simpler captcha service that uses an image to prevent spam bots. It is suggested to use “Captcha – ReCaptcha”.

title: Search
content:
Overview

The HUBzero platform uses Solr as the main search engine. Solr is a highly configurable search engine with many different options that control its behavior. Solr’s default configuration comes with a ton of helpful features which provide a high level of productivity out-of-the-box.

Solr is not implemented in all areas of the Hub, however, it will be expanded throughout the upcoming releases. The foundation of the integration will allow for basic search functionalities. The following search plugins are currently available:

  • Answers
  • Citations
  • Collections
  • Content
  • Courses
  • Forum
  • Groups
  • Members (public profile and public fields)
  • Projects
  • Publications
  • Resources
  • Tools
  • Wiki
  • Knowledge Base 

Query Syntax

Searching Fields:

Solr supports matching within a particular field. This means that one can specify a term to search for within a particular area of a document.

Available Search Fields:

  • title - filters search down to title results
  • author - filters search down to author results
  • description - filters search down to full-text results
  • path - filters search down to related path results
  • DOI - filters search if the object has a DOI issued

 

Partial Words:

The Hubzero implementation of Solr has not yet been tuned to understand complex phrases in the English language (or any other language for that matter). Therefore Solr sees the words “puppy” and “puppies” as two different concepts. Solr supports partial word matching through the use of the wildcard symbol, *. To perform a search for both “puppies” and “puppy” the query will read “pupp*”.

 

Complex Queries:

Solr comes with a query parser that understands Boolean search terms. This means that the keywords “OR” and “AND” can be used. When “OR” is used, Solr returns inclusive results. When “AND” is used, Solr returns exclusive results. For example, the query “cats OR dogs OR puppies OR pupp” will return any results that contain the words cats, dogs, puppies, or the partial word ‘pupp’.’.

To demonstrate the use of the keyword “AND”, consider the query of “cats AND dogs”. This means that Solr will only return the results that have both cats and dogs within the record. In this dataset, this was not a popular combination. More information about the Solr Query Syntax is available on their wiki: https://solr.apache.org/guide/6_6/the-standard-query-parser.html.

Search Results

A search result listing contains a few portions:

  1. Title - The title of the content Category - The plugin / facet of the data.
  2. Date - The date (usually created date) associated with the record.
  3. Author - Authors listed on the item.
  4. Tags - Hubzero tags applied to the item.
  5. Description - A snippet of all matching text in the record.
  6. Path - The path to the original item.

What is this "Feed" button?

Navigating to the What's New section of Resources or Knowledge Base, one can find a Feed button that spits out RSS feed. A user can take this feed and add it to their favorite page services or personal browser feed, depending on their use case. This way one can catch up on all the new resources and knowledge base articles that have been posted recently and stay on top of Hub activity.

title: Tags
content:
Overview

Tags are like keywords or category labels. Tags help you find content, events, and members which have something in common or similar interests. Tags can be added to groups, your profile, resources, wiki pages, and events. When creating or editing content, your profile, groups, etc. you can add or remove tags as you wish. If a tag does not exist, simply typing it in a Tags form field will create it and make it available for everyone to use on the Hub. Once a tag has been created, Hub search engines will pull the contribution documents and resources linked to that tag whenever a user searches a word related to a tag.

Creating a Tag

  1. Navigate to https://yourhub.org/
  2. Log in to the frontend of the Hub and access a section of the Hub where tags will be available
  3. Begin to edit the new media type​
  4. In the Tag text box, type in the phrase or word that the tag will be
  5. Once the project is saved, the new tag will be created

title: Tools
content:
Managing Tools

While Tools can only be managed through the tool pipeline,  tool sessions can be managed on the backend in the /administrator interface.

Managing the Maximum Open Tool Sessions per User

User session limits (and tool preferences) can be found by following these steps:

  1. Navigate to /administrator interface
  2. Hover over Components and from the drop-down select Tools
  3. Click on User Preferences
  4. Number of sessions is dictated by the session class
    1. Default Class = 3
      1. Add another class by clicking "Custom" class, then enter the number for the user
  5. If a user doesn't have an entry, you can create one for them

title: Components
content:
Introduction

The Components section will house all internal documentation that specifies details affiliated with various components.

Extendable Project Description Documentation

Functional Specification

Project description pages will have a setting to allow PlantingScience.org administrators to add custom fields including i) text fields, ii) tags, iii) urls, iv) choice boxes.

The users, including teachers and students, will be able to edit these items throughout the life of the project.

Even if already filled in, they will be able to go back and edit them more when they click on the edit description area for a project.

Each such fill­in item will have the capability to have a short description above it that appears in the project description edit area, but which is not present when the project description is viewed in the normal, non­edit mode.

Administrative Usage Instructions

Hub administrators are responsible for configuration of the Custom Description Template before Projects may utilize the feature. Projects created before this option has been configured may retroactively populate the Custom Description Template after the setup is complete.

Enabling Custom Description

Administrators may log into the administrative backend to configure this option. By default, this feature is turned off and must be enabled by going into Components >> Projects >> Options >> Setup >> Allow Users to Edit Project Settings? >> Yes ­ Use custom description

Creating the Custom Description Template

Once the custom description has been enabled, a new button will appear on the administrative toolbar under the Projects Component.

Clicking this button will direct the administrator to the form builder. Clicking on a field type will allow the administrator to configure the element’s properties such as name, options, and description.

In this example, the “Text” field type has been chosen.

 

Clicking “Save” or “Save and close will set the Custom Description Template hub­wide for all projects.

 

 

Non­administrator usage instructions

Project managers may edit the project’s information at any time. If the Custom Description Template is configured, a project manager role may fill in the information requested by administrators.

 

 

Project Information Non­edit mode (before updating)

To project members, the following information is presented by default. It is created when the project is in the setup state. This view is accessed from within the project by clicking on the “Info” tab on the side navigation bar. To edit the project information, click on the Edit Project button in the top right­hand corner.

 

 

Project Information ­ Edit Mode

Within edit mode, the Project Manager may edit the fields that are presented in the information section of the project settings. Notice there fields under the set “Edit Info” which are mandatory for all projects. Fields in the “Edit Extended Info” are those configured in the Custom Description Template.

 

 

After filling out the requested information, click “Save Changes” to save the project information.

 

 

Project Information Non­edit mode (after updating)

Once the project information is saved, it will appear in the Project information section.

HUBzero CMS Authentication - Fail2Ban Integration

Objective

To have the CMS handle user login banning in an attempt to deter brute force attacks.

 

CMS Configuration Page

The following settings are accessible from the CMS administrative backend.

These options are accessible by going to the User Menu ­ Members and Member Options.

User Password Reset Limit

The number of password resets per time period is limited. If the user attempts to reset their password at a threshold deemed by the HUB administrator as excessive, the following message is displayed.

User Failed Login Limit

The number of failed logins per time period is limited. If the user attempts to reset their password at a threshold deemed by the HUB administrator as excessive, the following message is displayed. This means that an individual's account is temporarily blocked until the time period expires.

IP­based Blocked User Limit

When the threshold of blocked user accounts per IP network is met, the CMS will trigger a Fail2Ban rule which will block incoming requests from an IP address for a period of time. This is the last line of defense as blocking an IP address may have unintended consequences ­ such as blocking a NAT­ed IP address which several valid users are using to access the hub.

Assumptions

This approach assumes that the system administrator has configured a jail and a system user account to execute (with sudo) Fail2Ban via the fail2ban­client utility.

On Debian Hosts, Fail2Ban should be version 0.9.5.

0.9.5­1~nd70+1 from http://neuro.debian.net/debian/ wheezy/main amd64 Packages

Setup & Configuration

There are a number of subsystems which need to be configured for this scheme to work properly.

 

sudo Configuration

A privileged user which can execute:

(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/fail2ban­client set hub­login banip [0­9.]* (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/fail2ban­client set hub­login unbanip [0­9.]*

This can be accomplished by adding a sudoers rule in /etc/sudoers.d/ that looks like:

www­data   ALL=(root)NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/fail2ban­client set hub­login banip [0­9.]*

Fail2Ban Configuration

The system administrator should configure Fail2Ban to create jails which the CMS can add offending IP address into. The amount of time that the ban is valid is configured in Fail2Ban.

The CMS will simply add IP addresses to the Fail2Ban jail which will trigger the Ban Action as specified in the rule set.

The following configuration are more of an example than anything. A seasoned system administrator will have crafted better rules.

[Sample] Jail Configuration

#

# JAILS

# /etc/fail2ban/jail.local

#

[hub­login] enabled  = true

port      = http,https filter      = hub­login

logpath = /var/log/messages banaction = hublogin­failure bantime = 600

findtime = 1

maxretry = 1

 

 

 

[Sample] Filter Configuration

/etc/fail2ban/filter.d/hub­login.conf

# Fail2Ban configuration file

#

[Definition]

 

 

# Option:  failregex

# Notes.:  Regexp to catch known spambots and software alike. Please verify

#           that it is your intent to block IPs which were driven by

#           abovementioned bots.

# Values:  TEXT

#

 

#We choose something that will never happen

# Since the CMS will control IP’s placed in the jails failregex = ^<HOST>thisfilterwillneverbefound

 

# Option:  ignoreregex

# Notes.:  regex to ignore. If this regex matches, the line is ignored.

# Values:  TEXT

#

ignoreregex =

 

 

 

[Sample] Action Configuration

# Fail2Ban configuration file

# cat /etc/fail2ban/action.d/hublogin­failure.conf [INCLUDES]

before = iptables­common.conf

 

 

[Definition]

 

# Option:   actionstart

# Notes.:   command executed once at the start of Fail2Ban.

# Values:   CMD

#

actionstart = iptables ­N fail2ban­hublogin

iptables ­A INPUT ­j DROP

iptables ­I INPUT ­p tcp ­j fail2ban­hublogin

 

# Option:   actionstop

# Notes.:   command executed once at the end of Fail2Ban

# Values:   CMD

#

actionstop = iptables ­D fail2ban­hublogin ­p tcp ­j fail2ban­hublogin iptables ­F fail2ban­hublogin

iptables ­X fail2ban­hublogin

 

# Option:   actioncheck

# Notes.:   command executed once before each actionban command

# Values:   CMD

#

actioncheck = iptables ­n ­L fail2ban­hublogin | grep ­q fail2ban­hublogin

 

# Option:   actionban

# Notes.:   command executed when banning an IP. Take care that the

#           command is executed with Fail2Ban user rights.

# Tags:     <ip>   IP address

#           <failures>   number of failures

#           <time>   unix timestamp of the ban time

# Values:   CMD

#

actionban = iptables ­I fail2ban­hublogin ­p tcp ­­dport 443 ­s <ip> ­j DROP

iptables ­I fail2ban­hublogin ­p tcp ­­dport

80 ­s <ip> ­j DROP

 

# Option:   actionunban

# Notes.:   command executed when unbanning an IP. Take care that the

#           command is executed with Fail2Ban user rights.

# Tags:     <ip>   IP address

#           <failures>   number of failures

#           <time>   unix timestamp of the ban time

# Values:   CMD

#

actionunban = iptables ­D fail2ban­hublogin ­p tcp ­­dport 443 ­s <ip> ­j DROP iptables ­D fail2ban­hublogin ­p tcp ­­dport 80 ­s <ip> ­j DROP

 

[Init]

 

# Defaut name of the chain

#

name = DEFAULT

 

# Option:   protocol

# Notes.:   internally used by config reader for interpolations.

# Values:   [ tcp | udp | icmp | all ] Default: tcp

#

protocol = tcp

 

# Option:   chain

# Notes     specifies the iptables chain to which the fail2ban rules should be

#           added

# Values:   STRING   Default: INPUT chain = INPUT

Developer Commentary

This feature has been designed primarily with HUBzero’s production environment in mind. While it would be nice to implement a generalized feature set for all distributions, it simply is not within the scope of this undertaking. This feature should be revisited frequently to determine whether or not it is appropriate to keep within the code base ­ or implemented as a plugin. I chose not to implement this as a plugin as I did not necessarily see the need to separate this from the HUBzero Authentication Plugin as it’s the only vector which is vulnerable to brute­force attacks which we have direct control over.

 

 

User Impact

When a large number of people intend on using the CMS, it may be wise to temporarily disable this feature (e.g. conference, class activity, etc). In the past, many conference goers have mistyped their password in a short period of time creating a false positive for normal Fail2Ban operation. This risk is mitigated by the fact that the number of blocked users is observed before triggering Fail2Ban.

 

This can be accomplished by turning this check off by going to the /administrator ­> Members ­> Member Options ­> Login Settings ­> Fail2Ban set to “Off”.

 

This implementation should give HUB owners more flexibility over their settings.

InCommon (Shibboleth)

NOTE: This is the internal documentation on how to implement InCommon for Purdue funded Hubs. Do not distribute this documentation to Hub users. There is documentation for Hubs outside of Purdue to follow. See: Non-Purdue Hub User InCommon Install

 

Aquire this information before beginning:

  1. Confirm that the Hub's email works (support@yourhub.org)
  2. Have the Hub PI's information
  3. Have the Hubzero contact point's information
  4. Know what organization is supporting the Hub (i.e. Purdue University - Main Campus)
  5. Confirm that the Hub has filled out their (yourhub.org/about) page

The task, then, is to combine these so that all the fields are complete, and the technical details all correspond exactly to what was generated in the second document by the software.

First, let’s clean up the generated metadata. A few things are going on that we need to unwind

  1. There is an XML comment at the very top that will soon be misleading, so we can delete it.
  2. The _ID=“some hex string” attribute is not actually used by InCommon, as seen in the example document, so we can delete that too.
  3. The XML namespacing is different in the generated document

OPTIONAL SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIAL ABOUT #3

Regarding the last, in XML you can define document that describe how particular tags work, and then link to those descriptions in documents using the tag in order to make their semantics self-documenting.

One of these descriptions is linked in the generated metadata and assigned a namespace of md: xmlns:md=“urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:metadata”`

These names are used so that even if two linked descriptions had two incompatible explanations of what an is, you can still specify that you’re talking about a particular definition with the prefix you see scattered throughout the document, md:

By leaving off the namespace, and simply using an attribute like xmlns=”(some URI that responds with the descriptive document)” you can set the global descriptive document for tags. If the opening tag here just read xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:metadata" none of the md: prefixes are required.

If you look at the very top of the InCommon metadata you can see that in the final home for the hub’s metadata this is exactly the case:

So, imagining that the document is situated as one entity among many in this large document, we can see that the md namespace is superfluous. Thus,

We don’t need the md: prefix on any of the tags, nor we need the xmlns:md=“urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:metadata”
